english: Hello, Minsu.
grammar: 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo) works morning, noon, and night — Korean's one all-day hello.

english: Hello! I'm Jieun.
Sujin, hello!
Hello, everyone!
Goodbye, Minsu.
grammar: 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo) to the person leaving; 안녕히 계세요 (gyeseyo) to the one staying.

english: Goodbye, teacher.
Nice to meet you, Junho.
grammar: 만나서 반가워요 (mannaseo bangawoyo) is one fixed phrase — 'glad to meet you.'

english: Nice to meet you too.
grammar: 도 replaces 은/는 to say 'too': 저도 (jeodo = me too).

english: I'm Sujin.
grammar: 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel: 수진이에요 (Sujin-ieyo), 민수예요 (Minsu-yeyo).

english: I'm Minsu.
What's your name?
grammar: Korean drops 'your' — 이름이 뭐예요? (ireumi mwoyeyo) is literally 'name is what?'

english: My name is Kim Minsu.
grammar: 제 (je) = my, the humble form of 저의: 제 이름 (je ireum = my name).

english: Are you Minsu?
grammar: No word for 'you' needed — use the name + 씨: 민수 씨예요? (Minsu ssi-yeyo = are you Minsu?)

english: Yes, I'm Minsu.
No, I'm not Minsu.
I'm Michael.
I'm Anna.
Sujin, this is my friend.
grammar: 이쪽 (ijjok = this side) politely introduces a friend or equal: 이쪽은 제 친구예요.

english: This is Teacher Park.
grammar: -세요 respects the person you talk about: 선생님이세요 (seonsaengnim-iseyo = is [my] teacher).

english: My younger sibling is a student.
What country are you from?
grammar: 어느 나라 사람이에요? (eoneu nara saramieyo) — literally 'which country person?' — asks nationality.

english: I'm Korean.
I'm British.
I'm American.
Minsu is Korean.
grammar: 은/는 marks the topic — 은 after consonants, 는 after vowels: 저는 (jeoneun), 씨는 (ssi-neun).

english: Is Jieun Korean too?
grammar: Yes/no questions keep the same words — just a rising tone: 사람이에요? (saramieyo?)

english: No, Jieun is American.
I'm not Chinese.
grammar: 'Is not X' = X이/가 아니에요: 중국 사람이 아니에요 (sarami anieyo = am not Chinese).

english: Is Junho Japanese?
I live in Seoul.
What do you do for work?
grammar: 무슨 일 해요? (museun il haeyo) — literally 'what work do you do?' — the natural way to ask a job.

english: I'm a student.
I'm a university student.
I'm a teacher.
grammar: 교사 (gyosa) = teacher as a job title; 선생님 honors OTHERS — never use it for yourself.

english: I'm an office worker.
Sujin is a doctor.
Junho is a nurse.
Is Jieun a singer?
No, Jieun is an actor.
I'm not a student.
Minsu is not a cook.
I'm a journalist.
Thank you, teacher.
grammar: 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is formal-polite — the safe thank-you for staff, elders, strangers.

english: Thank you very much.
grammar: 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is formal 합니다체 (hamnida-che) — thanks to strangers stays formal.

english: Oh, I'm sorry.
grammar: 죄송해요 (joesonghaeyo) is the everyday polite 'sorry' — bump into someone, say it.

english: I'm really sorry.
It's okay, Minsu.
grammar: 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) covers 'it's fine,' 'no problem,' and 'I'm OK' — one word, many uses.

english: Yes, I'm fine.
Sujin, are you okay?
Not at all, it's fine.
grammar: 아니에요 (anieyo) after thanks = 'not at all / you're welcome.'

english: Excuse me, just a moment.
grammar: 저기요 (jeogiyo) hails a stranger or waiter; 잠시만요 (jamsimanyo) = 'just a moment, please.'

english: Thanks a lot, Jieun. (friendly polite)
grammar: 고마워요 (gomawoyo) = warm everyday thanks; 감사합니다 is the formal notch up.

english: Nice to meet you, Michael.
Jieun, are you a student?
Yes, I'm a student.
grammar: Korean drops pronouns when clear — 학생이에요 (haksaengieyo) alone means 'I'm a student.'

english: No, I'm an office worker.
Michael, are you American?
Yes, I'm American.
No, I'm Canadian.
Yes, that's right.
grammar: 맞아요 (majayo) = 'that's right' — the everyday way to confirm.

english: What's this?
grammar: 이 = near me, 그 = near you, 저 = far from both: 이거/그거/저거 (igeo/geugeo/jeogeo).

english: What's that (by you)?
What's that (over there)?
This is coffee.
That's my bag.
That over there is our house.
grammar: Koreans say 우리 (uri = our) even for their own home or family: 우리 집 (uri jip = my house).

english: Is this water?
No, that's tea.
What's this in Korean?
grammar: (으)로 = 'in / by means of': 한국어로 (hangugeo-ro) = in Korean.

english: Do you have a question?
grammar: Korean 'have' is 'exist': 있어요 (isseoyo) = there is / I have; 없어요 (eopseoyo) = don't have.

english: Yes, I have a question.
Minsu, do you have time?
No, I don't have time.
I don't have an umbrella.
Do you have your passport?
I drink water.
grammar: 을/를 marks the object — 을 after a consonant, 를 after a vowel: 물을 마셔요 (mur-eul masyeoyo = I drink water).

english: I drink coffee.
I eat rice.
I eat bread.
I read a book.
I buy apples.
grammar: 사요 means 'buy' — one letter from 싸요 (ssayo = cheap): 사과를 사요 (sagwa-reul sayo = I buy apples).

english: I watch a movie.
I drink milk.
I like kimchi.
grammar: 좋아해요 'like' takes an object with 을/를: 김치를 좋아해요 (gimchi-reul joahaeyo = I like kimchi).

english: I meet a friend.
I read the newspaper.
I drink tea.
I watch television.
I buy fruit.
I listen to music.
grammar: 들어요 covers both 'listen' and 'hear': 음악을 들어요 (eumag-eul deureoyo = I listen to music).

english: I like coffee.
grammar: 은/는 sets the topic — 'as for X': 저는 커피를 좋아해요 (jeo-neun keopi-reul joahaeyo).

english: My younger sibling drinks milk.
A friend is coming.
grammar: 이/가 marks the subject — 가 after a vowel, 이 after a consonant: 친구가 와요 (chingu-ga wayo).

english: The bus is coming.
I don't have time.
I don't have money.
There is water.
I go to school.
grammar: 에 marks a destination or a time: 학교에 가요 (hakgyo-e gayo = I go to school).

english: I go to the market.
I'm at home.
I drink coffee at a cafe.
grammar: 에서 marks where an action happens: 카페에서 마셔요 (kape-eseo masyeoyo = I drink at a cafe).

english: I cook at home.
I study at the library.
I work at a company.
I eat at a restaurant.
I drink coffee too.
grammar: 도 means 'too' and replaces 은/는 or 을/를: 저도 마셔요 (jeo-do masyeoyo = I drink too).

english: My younger sibling goes to school too.
I buy bread too.
I work today too.
I don't eat meat.
grammar: 안 goes right before the verb: 안 먹어요 (an meogeoyo = I don't eat).

english: I don't drink coffee.
I don't watch television.
I'm not studying today.
grammar: With 하다 verbs, 안 slips inside: 공부 안 해요 (gongbu an haeyo = I don't study).

english: I can't go today.
grammar: 못 = can't, 안 = don't: 못 가요 (mot gayo = I can't go).

english: I can't eat fish.
I exercise in the morning.
I take a walk in the park.
I drink juice.
I eat ramyeon.
grammar: 라면을 먹어요 (ramyeon-eul meogeoyo) — 라면 is instant noodles, Korea's favorite late-night meal.

english: I make a cake.
I buy a bag.
I'm looking for my umbrella.
grammar: 찾아요 means both 'look for' and 'find': 우산을 찾아요 (usan-eul chajayo = I look for my umbrella).

english: I put on clothes.
I buy shoes.
I open the door.
I close the window.
I wash my hands.
grammar: 씻어요 'wash' works for hands, face, and fruit: 손을 씻어요 (son-eul ssiseoyo = I wash my hands).

english: I look at photos.
I learn Korean.
I write a letter.
I write my name.
I take the bus.
grammar: 타요 'take/ride' uses 을/를: 버스를 타요 (beoseu-reul tayo = I take the bus).

english: I take the subway.
I buy a ticket.
I buy vegetables at the supermarket.
My younger sibling reads the newspaper.
grammar: 봐요 covers watching and casual reading: 신문을 봐요 (sinmun-eul bwayo = I read the paper).

english: My older sister likes cooking.
grammar: 언니 (eonni) = a woman's older sister; men say 누나 (nuna).

english: My friend doesn't drink coffee.
Is there milk?
Where is the bathroom?
grammar: The survival question: 화장실이 어디에 있어요? (hwajangsil-i eodi-e isseoyo? = where is the bathroom?)

english: What are you buying at the store?
grammar: In speech 을/를 often drops: 뭐를 사요? → 뭐 사요? (mwo sayo? = what are you buying?)

english: Do you like gimbap?
grammar: 김밥 (gimbap) is seaweed rice rolls: 김밥을 좋아해요? (gimbab-eul joahaeyo? = do you like gimbap?)

english: Yes, I really like gimbap.
No, I don't like fish.
Do you drink beer?
No, I can't drink beer.
I use a computer at work.
grammar: 써요 means 'write' and also 'use': 컴퓨터를 써요 (keompyuteo-reul sseoyo = I use a computer).

english: I clean the room.
I need coffee.
grammar: 필요해요 'need' takes 이/가, not 을/를: 커피가 필요해요 (keopi-ga piryohaeyo = I need coffee).

english: I meet my family on the weekend.
What are you doing now?
grammar: Questions keep the same -요 form — only intonation rises: 지금 뭐 해요? (jigeum mwo haeyo? = what are you doing now?)

english: What are you eating?
What are you doing today?
What is that?
grammar: After a vowel the copula is 예요: 이거 뭐예요? (igeo mwoyeyo? = what is this?)

english: What is the name of this song?
What are you doing on the weekend?
Where are you going?
grammar: 어디 (eodi = where) usually drops its particle in speech: 어디 가요? (eodi gayo? = where are you going?)

english: Where do you live?
Where do you work?
Where is the bathroom?
grammar: Ask where something is with -이/가 어디예요?: 화장실이 어디예요? (hwajangsiri eodiyeyo?)

english: Where is the station?
Where are you now?
Who is that person?
Who are you waiting for?
Who do you live with?
Who is Minsu?
grammar: Korean avoids 'you' — use the person's name + 씨: 민수 씨 (Minsu-ssi = Minsu).

english: When are you coming?
When does it start?
When is your birthday?
grammar: Ask when something is with -이/가 언제예요?: 생일이 언제예요? (saengiri eonjeyeyo?)

english: When is the meeting?
Why are you laughing?
Why aren't you eating?
Why are you busy?
How do I get there?
grammar: 어떻게 (eotteoke) = how: 어떻게 가요? (eotteoke gayo? = how do I get there?)

english: How do I get to the station?
How is the weather?
grammar: 어때요? (eottaeyo?) asks 'how is …?': 날씨가 어때요? (nalssiga eottaeyo? = how is the weather?)

english: How is work?
I drink one cup of coffee.
grammar: Count things with native numbers + a counter: 한 잔 (han jan = one cup), 두 명 (du myeong = two people).

english: I eat one apple.
I buy two pieces of bread.
Two friends are coming.
There are five people in my family.
How many people are there?
grammar: 몇 + counter asks 'how many': 몇 명이에요? (myeot myeong-ieyo? = how many people?)

english: How many do you have?
I have two younger siblings.
I have two bags.
How much is this?
grammar: 얼마예요? (eolmayeyo?) = 'how much is it?' — the everyday shopping question.

english: How much is the coffee?
It is 5,000 won.
grammar: Money uses Sino-Korean numbers + 원: 오천 원이에요 (ocheon won-ieyo = it is 5,000 won).

english: It is 10,000 won.
grammar: Korean counts big money in units of 만 (man = 10,000): 만 원 (man won = 10,000 won).

english: The bread is 2,000 won.
The water is 1,000 won.
The ticket is 30,000 won.
It is too expensive.
This store is cheap.
I do not have money right now.
Do you have money now?
What time is it now?
grammar: Ask the time with 몇 시예요? (myeot siyeyo? = what time is it?)

english: It is three o'clock.
grammar: Hours use native numbers + 시: 세 시 (se si = three o'clock), 한 시 (han si = one o'clock).

english: It is one o'clock.
It is half past two.
grammar: 반 (ban) = half: 두 시 반 (du si ban = half past two).

english: I get up at six o'clock.
grammar: 에 after a time means 'at': 여섯 시에 일어나요 (yeoseot si-e ireonayo = I get up at six).

english: It ends at five o'clock.
There is a meeting at two o'clock.
What time does it start?
What time do you go to sleep?
I eat dinner at seven o'clock.
What time do you arrive?
It takes one hour.
grammar: 걸려요 (geollyeoyo) = 'it takes (time)': 한 시간 걸려요 (han sigan geollyeoyo = it takes an hour).

english: The bus comes at ten o'clock.
What day is it today?
grammar: 무슨 (museun) = 'what kind of': 무슨 요일이에요? (museun yoirieyo? = what day is it?)

english: Today is Friday.
grammar: After a consonant the copula is 이에요: 금요일이에요 (geumyoirieyo = it is Friday).

english: Tomorrow is Saturday.
I work on Monday.
grammar: Days of the week take 에 (on): 월요일에 일해요 (woryoire ilhaeyo = I work on Monday).

english: I exercise on Tuesday.
I learn Korean on Wednesday.
I meet a friend on Thursday.
I cook at home on Sunday.
I watch a movie on the weekend.
I am going tomorrow.
grammar: The present tense covers the near future: 내일 가요 (naeil gayo = I am going tomorrow).

english: A friend is coming tomorrow.
I am going to school today.
I am going home now.
I am going to Seoul tomorrow.
I am starting now.
I go to school in the morning.
grammar: 에 marks the destination: 학교에 가요 (hakgyo-e gayo = I go to school).

english: My younger sibling is coming home.
Today I go to the office.
A friend comes to our house.
grammar: 와요 = motion toward the speaker; 가요 = away: 집에 와요 (jib-e wayo = comes home).

english: Tomorrow I go to the market.
I come to school in the morning.
grammar: Say 와요 (wayo) only while you're at school — 오다 (oda) means coming to where the speaker is now.

english: I go to the office by bus.
grammar: 로 = by (a means of transport): 버스로 가요 (beoseu-ro gayo = I go by bus).

english: On the weekend I go to the park.
I go to a café with a friend.
grammar: 랑 = with (someone), friendly in speech: 친구랑 (chingu-rang = with a friend).

english: I'm going to the bank now.
Mom comes home.
In the evening I go to a restaurant.
I go to the airport by subway.
I work at the office on Mondays.
grammar: 에서 marks where an action happens: 회사에서 일해요 (hoesa-eseo ilhaeyo = I work at the office).

english: I study at the library on weekends.
I drink coffee with a friend at a café.
In the evening I eat at a restaurant.
I am cooking at home today.
I exercise in the park.
I buy fruit at the supermarket.
I learn Korean at school.
I listen to music at home.
I buy a book at the bookstore.
I exercise every day.
grammar: Noun + 해요 makes an action verb: 운동해요 (undonghaeyo = I exercise, lit. do exercise).

english: I study in the morning.
I call mom.
grammar: 한테 = to (a person): 엄마한테 전화해요 (eomma-hante jeonhwahaeyo = I call mom).

english: I cook in the evening.
I shop on the weekend.
I clean today.
I exercise together with a friend.
grammar: 같이 = together: 같이 운동해요 (gachi undonghaeyo = we exercise together).

english: I make phone calls at the office.
I study Korean every day.
Dad cooks.
I'm doing homework now.
I meet a friend on the weekend.
I take a walk in the evening.
I take a shower at night.
I like coffee.
grammar: To like something: noun + 을/를 좋아해요: 커피를 좋아해요 (keopi-reul joahaeyo = I like coffee).

english: I like Korean food.
Our family likes kimchi.
Do you like exercise?
grammar: A question keeps the same words — just raise the tone: 좋아해요? (joahaeyo? = do you like it?)

english: I like dogs.
My friend likes movies.
I really like music.
My younger sibling likes games.
Water, please.
grammar: Ordering: thing + 주세요: 물 주세요 (mul juseyo = water, please). A fixed phrase — use it as is.

english: Coffee, please.
The menu, please.
Bibimbap, please.
Some kimchi, please.
grammar: 좀 softens a request: 김치 좀 주세요 (gimchi jom juseyo = some kimchi, please).

english: The receipt, please.
Where is the bathroom here?
grammar: 어디에 있어요? = where is …?: 화장실이 어디에 있어요? (hwajangsil-i eodi-e isseoyo?)

english: It's here.
grammar: 여기 = here, 거기 = there (by you), 저기 = over there: 여기에 있어요 (yeogi-e isseoyo = it's here).

english: The bank is over there.
Where is the subway station?
The hospital is next to the school.
grammar: 옆에 = next to: 학교 옆에 있어요 (hakgyo yeop-e isseoyo = it's next to the school).

english: The café is in front of the bank.
The convenience store is near my house.
grammar: 근처에 = near: 집 근처에 있어요 (jip geuncheo-e isseoyo = it's near my house).

english: My bag is there.
grammar: 제 = my (humble, from 저): 제 가방 (je gabang = my bag).

english: Where is the park?
The key isn't here.
The hotel is near the airport.
The cat is at home.
grammar: To say where something is: place + 에 있어요: 집에 있어요 (jib-e isseoyo = it's at home).

english: The weather is good.
grammar: Korean adjectives work like verbs — no 'is' needed: 좋아요 (joayo) alone means 'it's good'.

english: The food at this restaurant is really good.
The bulgogi is delicious.
This bag is too expensive.
grammar: 너무 = too/so: 너무 비싸요 (neomu bissayo = it's too expensive).

english: These clothes are cheap.
Our house is big.
My room is small.
The department store is expensive.
This park is really nice.
The school is big.
The airport is far from home.
grammar: 에서 also means 'from' with distance: 집에서 멀어요 (jib-eseo meoreoyo = far from home).

english: The subway station is close to my house.
What did you do yesterday?
grammar: 어제 뭐 했어요? (eoje mwo haesseoyo) — the go-to small-talk opener about yesterday.

english: I met a friend yesterday.
grammar: 만나다 takes 을/를, not 'with': 친구를 만났어요 (chingureul mannasseoyo = met a friend).

english: I was at home yesterday.
What did you eat yesterday?
I ate bulgogi yesterday.
Where did you go yesterday?
I went to the market yesterday.
I didn't work yesterday.
grammar: 는 after a time word adds contrast: 어제는 (eojeneun = as for yesterday).

english: I was so busy yesterday.
I watched a movie yesterday.
This morning I got up at six.
grammar: Clock times take 에: 여섯 시에 일어났어요 (yeoseot sie ireonasseoyo = got up at six).

english: I showered in the morning.
I ate bread in the morning.
I drank coffee in the morning.
I couldn't eat breakfast today.
grammar: 아침 (achim) means morning AND breakfast — 아침을 먹다 = eat breakfast.

english: I exercised in the morning.
I left home at seven.
I took the bus.
grammar: 타다 takes 을/를: 버스를 탔어요 (beoseureul tasseoyo = took the bus).

english: I was late for work today.
grammar: 늦다 takes 에 for what you are late to: 회사에 늦었어요 (hoesae neujeosseoyo = was late for work).

english: I read the newspaper in the morning.
What did you do on the weekend?
grammar: 주말에 뭐 했어요? (jumare mwo haesseoyo) — Monday's standard icebreaker.

english: I rested well at home on the weekend.
grammar: 쉬다 (swida = to rest): 잘 쉬었어요? is how you ask 'did you have a good break?'

english: On Saturday I walked in the park.
On Sunday I got up late.
grammar: 늦게 (neutge = late) sits right before the verb: 늦게 일어났어요 = got up late.

english: I went to Busan on the weekend.
I saw the sea.
I took lots of photos.
grammar: Korean 'shoots' photos: 사진을 찍어요 (sajineul jjigeoyo = take a photo).

english: On the weekend I watched a drama at home.
On Friday evening I ate fried chicken.
grammar: 치킨 (chikin) = fried chicken, a Friday-night institution in Korea.

english: The weekend was really fun.
grammar: 재미있었어요 (jaemiisseosseoyo = it was fun) — the all-purpose good-time verdict.

english: What did you have for lunch today?
I ate gimbap for lunch.
I ate ramyeon in the evening.
I didn't eat dinner yesterday.
I ate bibimbap at a restaurant.
I ate samgyeopsal with a friend.
grammar: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal = pork belly) is grilled at the table — Korea's favorite group dinner.

english: I made a cake.
I drank a lot of water.
grammar: 많이 (mani = a lot) goes before the verb: 많이 마셨어요 = drank a lot.

english: I drank one beer yesterday.
The food was really delicious.
What did you buy yesterday?
grammar: 뭐 샀어요? (mwo sasseoyo = what did you buy?) — 뭐 usually drops its particle in speech.

english: I bought milk at the mart.
I bought clothes at the department store.
The shoes were too expensive.
grammar: Korean adjectives take past endings like verbs: 비쌌어요 (bissasseoyo = was expensive).

english: I bought a present.
I spent all the money.
grammar: 쓰다 means write, use, AND spend: 돈을 다 썼어요 (doneul da sseosseoyo = spent all the money).

english: I bought fruit at the market.
I couldn't buy the bag.
I got the receipt.
These clothes were 10,000 won.
grammar: Past 'it was X': 이었어요 after consonants — 만 원이었어요 (man wonieosseoyo = it was 10,000 won).

english: I went to work at nine today.
grammar: 출근하다 (chulgeunhada = go to work), 퇴근하다 = leave work — one verb for each.

english: There was a meeting yesterday.
The meeting started at three.
grammar: 시작하다 (sijakada) works both ways: 회의가 시작했어요 = it started; 회의를 시작했어요 = (I) started it.

english: I had a lot of work today.
grammar: 일이 많았어요 (iri manasseoyo), literally 'work was many' — Korean for 'I was swamped.'

english: I wrote an email.
I prepared a presentation.
The presentation went well.
grammar: 잘 됐어요 (jal dwaesseoyo) = 'it went well' — also the response to good news: 'great!'

english: I worked until late yesterday.
grammar: 까지 (kkaji = until): 늦게까지 일했어요 = worked until late.

english: I left work at six.
I met a visitor at the office.
I didn't go to work today.
I wrote a report.
There was an exam on Monday.
The exam was hard.
There were many questions.
Last year I went to Korea.
grammar: 작년 (jangnyeon = last year), 내년 = next year — 년 is the 'year' piece.

english: I stayed in Seoul for a week.
grammar: Duration needs no particle: 일주일 있었어요 (iljuil isseosseoyo = stayed a week).

english: I went by plane.
grammar: (으)로 marks the means: 비행기로 (bihaenggiro = by plane).

english: The hotel was very good.
I looked around the museum.
grammar: 구경하다 (gugyeonghada) = look around for fun — museums, markets, anywhere.

english: Last week I went to Jeju Island.
The weather in Jeju was really nice.
I swam in the sea.
I took the train for the first time.
grammar: 처음 (cheoeum = first time) drops in before the verb: 처음 탔어요 = rode it for the first time.

english: I went to the hotel by taxi.
I got lost.
grammar: 길을 잃었어요 (gireul ireosseoyo) = 'I got lost' — literally 'lost the road.'

english: I ate a lot of Korean food.
The trip was really fun.
I bought the tickets in advance.
grammar: 미리 (miri = in advance): 미리 샀어요 = bought ahead of time.

english: I arrived at the airport early.
Last weekend I met my parents.
grammar: 지난 (jinan = last): 지난 주말 = last weekend, 지난달 = last month.

english: I went to Grandma's house.
Grandma made dinner.
grammar: Honor elders with -(으)시-: 할머니가 만드셨어요 (mandeusyeosseoyo = made, honorific).

english: I had dinner together with my family.
grammar: (이)랑 같이 (irang gachi = together with): 가족이랑 같이 = with my family.

english: My younger sibling came home yesterday.
I called my mom.
Dad bought a cake.
grammar: Parents get -(으)시- too: 사셨어요 (sasyeosseoyo = bought, honorific).

english: My older sister got married.
grammar: 결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) covers both 'got married' and 'is married.'

english: We moved to Seoul last month.
A friend gave me a present.
I went to karaoke with a friend.
grammar: 노래방 (noraebang) = private karaoke room — 방 means room.

english: I hung out with a friend on the weekend.
grammar: 놀다 (nolda) isn't just for kids — adults use 놀았어요 for 'hung out.'

english: We had a birthday party.
I invited a friend to my house.
grammar: 초대하다 (chodaehada = invite): 집에 초대했어요 = invited (them) over.

english: I laughed so much yesterday.
How was the weather yesterday?
grammar: 어땠어요? (eottaesseoyo = how was it?) — the past of 어때요, perfect for any recap.

english: It rained yesterday.
grammar: Rain 'comes' in Korean: 비가 왔어요 (biga wasseoyo = it rained).

english: It snowed last week.
grammar: 눈 (nun) = snow and also 'eye' — 눈이 왔어요 can only mean it snowed.

english: It was really cold yesterday.
It was too hot last weekend.
It was cloudy in the morning.
The weather was clear in the afternoon.
grammar: 맑다 (makda) = clear skies: 날씨가 맑았어요 = the weather was clear.

english: I was sick yesterday.
grammar: 몸이 아팠어요 (momi apasseoyo) = 'I was sick' — literally 'my body hurt.'

english: I had a headache.
I went to the hospital.
I took medicine.
grammar: Korean 'eats' medicine: 약을 먹어요 (yageul meogeoyo = take medicine).

english: I went to bed early yesterday.
Did you sleep well?
grammar: 잘 잤어요? (jal jasseoyo) = 'did you sleep well?' — a warm morning greeting at home.

english: Yes, I slept well.
I slept ten hours yesterday.
grammar: 시간 (sigan) counts hours with native numbers: 열 시간 (yeol sigan = ten hours).

english: I was so tired.
grammar: 피곤했어요 (pigonhaesseoyo = was tired) — the standard end-of-day report.

english: I felt good.
The movie was really sad.
I listened to music yesterday.
I went to a concert.
The concert was really good.
I read two books over the weekend.
grammar: 권 (gwon) counts books: 두 권 (du gwon = two volumes) — native numbers before counters.

english: That book was a bit hard.
grammar: 조금 (jogeum = a little) softens anything: 조금 어려웠어요 = it was a bit hard.

english: I studied Korean for two hours yesterday.
I learned a lot of words.
I finished all my homework.
grammar: 다 (da = all) goes right before the verb: 다 했어요 = did it all.

english: I didn't play games yesterday.
I watched a little TV.
I wrote a letter to a friend.
It was a really good day.
grammar: 하루 (haru = a day, the day): 하루가 정말 좋았어요 = it was a really good day.

english: What are you going to do tomorrow?
grammar: (으)ㄹ 거예요 (l geoyeyo) = 'going to' — Korean's everyday future: 할 거예요 = will do.

english: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
What are you going to do on the weekend?
I'll rest at home this weekend.
grammar: 쉴 거예요 (swil geoyeyo = will rest) — 집에서 쉬다 is the classic weekend plan.

english: Where will you go tomorrow?
I'll go to the library tomorrow.
What will you eat for dinner?
I'll eat pizza for dinner.
I'll go to bed early tonight.
What time will you get up tomorrow?
I'll get up at eight tomorrow.
I'll walk in the park in the morning.
I'll go to the bank tomorrow.
I'll buy clothes tomorrow.
I'll clean my room tomorrow.
A friend is coming the day after tomorrow.
grammar: 모레 (more) = the day after tomorrow — one word, no 'tomorrow's tomorrow' needed.

english: I'll make Korean food tomorrow.
I'll go to work early tomorrow.
I'm not going to cook tomorrow.
grammar: Negate futures with 안 before the verb: 안 할 거예요 (an hal geoyeyo = won't do).

english: I'll exercise tomorrow evening.
I'll watch a movie on Saturday.
I'll get up late on Sunday.
I'll go to the mountains this weekend.
grammar: 산에 가다 (sane gada) = go hiking — Koreans say 'go to the mountain.'

english: I'll hang out with a friend on the weekend.
I'll go shopping this weekend.
grammar: 이번 (ibeon = this coming): 이번 주말 = this weekend, 이번 주 = this week.

english: I'll do laundry on Saturday.
I'll see Grandpa on Sunday.
We'll have a party this weekend.
On Friday I'll drink beer with a friend.
I'll get a good rest this weekend.
grammar: 푹 (puk) = deeply, only with rest or sleep: 푹 쉴 거예요 = I'll rest up properly.

english: I'm going to Korea next year.
grammar: 내년에 (naenyeone = next year): future time words still take 에.

english: I'll travel in the summer.
I'll go to Busan next week.
We'll go by train.
I'll book a hotel.
grammar: 예약하다 (yeyakada = reserve, book) — hotels, restaurants, tickets alike.

english: I'll swim in the sea.
I'll take lots of photos.
We'll be in Jeju for three days.
grammar: Days of duration use Sino numbers: 삼 일 (sam il = three days).

english: I'll buy the tickets tomorrow.
The plane will depart at nine.
grammar: 출발하다 (chulbalhada = depart), 도착하다 = arrive — a natural pair.

english: I'll go to the airport early.
I'll pack my bags tonight.
grammar: 짐을 싸다 (jimeul ssada) = pack your bags — same 싸다 as 'cheap,' context decides.

english: We'll look around the market.
I'll go together with my parents.
The vacation will be really fun.
grammar: 휴가 (hyuga) = your days off; 여행 (yeohaeng) = the trip you take on them.

english: There will be a meeting tomorrow.
The meeting will start at ten.
I'll write the report tomorrow.
I'll give a presentation next week.
grammar: 발표하다 (balpyohada = give a presentation): 다음 주에 발표할 거예요.

english: I'll work late today.
I'll start a new project tomorrow.
grammar: 새 (sae = new) sits before its noun: 새 프로젝트 = a new project.

english: I'll leave work early on Friday.

target: 다음 달에 새 일을 시작할 거예요.
english: I'll start a new job next month.
grammar: 다음 (daeum = next): 다음 달 = next month, 다음 주 = next week.

english: I'll send the email today.
grammar: 보내다 (bonaeda = send) works for mail, texts, and people alike.

english: I'll eat lunch at the office tomorrow.
I'll be busy on Monday.
The meeting will be long.
The boss will come tomorrow.
grammar: 님 (nim) honors titles, and the verb takes 시: 사장님이 오실 거예요 (osil geoyeyo).

english: I'll work in Seoul next week.
I'm going to buy a new computer.
What will the weather be like tomorrow?
grammar: 어떨 거예요? (eotteol geoyeyo = how will it be?) — 어때요's future twin.

english: It will rain tomorrow.
grammar: (으)ㄹ 거예요 also predicts: 비가 올 거예요 (biga ol geoyeyo = it'll rain).

english: It will snow on the weekend.
It will be cold tomorrow.
It will be hot next week.
It will be cloudy in the afternoon.
It will be clear tomorrow morning.
The weather will be nice tomorrow.
Winter will come soon.
grammar: 곧 (got = soon): 곧 올 거예요 = it'll come soon.

english: You'll need an umbrella tomorrow.
I'll definitely call tomorrow.
grammar: 꼭 (kkok = definitely) turns plans into promises: 꼭 갈 거예요 = I'll definitely go.

english: I'll keep my promise.
grammar: 약속 (yaksok) = both 'promise' and 'plans with someone' — 약속이 있어요 = I have plans.

english: I'm going to exercise every day.
This year I'll study Korean hard.
grammar: 열심히 (yeolsimhi = hard, diligently): 열심히 공부할 거예요 = I'll study hard.

english: I'm not going to drink coffee.
I'm going to get up early every day.
I'm going to save money.
grammar: 돈을 모으다 (doneul moeuda) = save money — literally 'gather' it.

english: I'm going to read a lot of books.
I won't play games at night.
Starting tomorrow, I'll start exercising.
grammar: 부터 (buteo = starting from): 내일부터 = from tomorrow on.

english: I'll tidy my room this week.
I'm going to make Korean friends.
grammar: 친구를 사귀다 (chingureul sagwida) = make friends — never 만들다 for people.

english: I'll go to my parents' house on the weekend.
Mom is going to make galbi.
grammar: 갈비 (galbi) = marinated short ribs, the family-dinner classic.

english: I'm going on a trip with my family.
My younger sibling is coming next week.
I'll buy a cake for Dad's birthday.
I'm going to call Grandma.
My older sister is getting married next year.
The wedding will be in the spring.
grammar: Seasons take 에: 봄에 (bome = in spring).

english: We're moving next month.

target: 새 집이 학교 근처에 있을 거예요.
english: The new house will be near the school.
I'll have dinner with my family.
I'll give my younger sibling a present.

target: 오늘 밤에 시험 공부를 할 거예요.
english: I'll study for the exam tonight.
grammar: 시험 공부 (siheom gongbu) = studying FOR an exam — nouns stack directly in Korean.

english: I'll learn new words every day.
I'm going to watch Korean dramas.
I'll learn Korean through songs.
I'll take an exam next week.
grammar: Korean 'sees' exams: 시험을 봐요 (siheomeul bwayo = take a test).

english: The exam will be easy.
I'll ask the teacher.
I'll study at the library for three hours.
Class will start at nine.
I'll practice hard.
Next year I'll be good at Korean.
grammar: 잘하다 (jalhada) = be good at: 한국어를 잘해요 = speaks Korean well.

english: What are you doing this evening?
I'll watch a drama in the evening.
I'll shower at night.
I'll eat dinner at seven.
A friend will call in the evening.
I'll listen to music tonight.
I'll go to bed at eleven.
When will you come?
grammar: 언제 (eonje = when) never takes 에: 언제 올 거예요? = when will you come?

english: I'll arrive at three.
Who is coming?
grammar: 누구 + 가 contracts: 누가 (nuga = who, as the subject).

english: Sujin will come.
Where will we meet?
We'll meet in front of the cafe.
grammar: Meeting spots take 에서: 앞에서 만날 거예요 (apeseo mannal geoyeyo = we'll meet in front).

english: What time will it end?
The movie will end at nine.
How long will it take?
grammar: 얼마나 (eolmana = how long/much): 얼마나 걸릴 거예요? = how long will it take?

english: It will take thirty minutes.
grammar: 분 (bun = minutes) takes Sino numbers: 삼십 분 (samsip bun = 30 minutes).

english: The train will depart soon.
Everything will be okay.
grammar: 다 잘 될 거예요 (da jal doel geoyeyo) — Korea's favorite reassurance: 'it'll all work out.'

english: See you tomorrow!
grammar: 내일 봐요 (naeil bwayo = see you tomorrow) — present form, future meaning.

english: I'm so hungry right now.
grammar: 배고파요 (baegopayo = I'm hungry) — no pronoun needed; Korean drops "I".

english: I didn't eat breakfast.
grammar: 안 before the verb = didn't: 안 먹었어요 (an meogeosseoyo = didn't eat).

english: Did you have lunch?
grammar: 점심 먹었어요? (jeomsim meogeosseoyo) doubles as a friendly greeting, like "how's it going?"

english: No, I haven't eaten yet.
I'm thirsty. Some water, please.
grammar: 목말라요 (mongmallayo = I'm thirsty) — 목 (throat) + 마르다 (to be dry).

english: Have you had dinner?
Yes, I already ate.
What's for lunch today?
There are lots of restaurants near the office.
This restaurant is famous for bulgogi.
Is there a restaurant near here?
What's good here?
grammar: 뭐가 맛있어요? (mwoga masisseoyo = what's tasty?) — ask staff; they love recommending.

english: The pork belly here is really delicious.
grammar: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal = pork belly) — 삼 (three) layers of meat and fat.

english: I recommend the kimchi stew.
This place is famous for cold noodles.
grammar: 집 (jip = house) also means a go-to eatery: 냉면 집 = a naengmyeon place.

english: I eat Korean food often.
Where is the menu?
What food do you like?
I really love tteokbokki.
How many people altogether?
grammar: 명 (myeong) counts people with native numbers: 두 명 (du myeong = two people).

english: Two people.
Do you have a table?
Two servings of pork belly, please.
grammar: 인분 (inbun = serving) takes Sino numbers: 2인분 (i-inbun = two servings).

english: One soybean-paste stew, please.
grammar: Ordering with 하나 (hana = one) after the dish name is the everyday pattern.

english: Water is self-serve.
grammar: 셀프 (selpeu = self-serve) — at many Korean restaurants you fetch water yourself.

english: The side dishes are free.
grammar: 반찬 (banchan = side dishes) come free — and usually refillable.

english: More side dishes, please.
Two rolls of gimbap, please.
grammar: 줄 (jul = roll/line) counts gimbap: 두 줄 (du jul = two rolls).

english: What are you going to order?
grammar: 시키다 (sikida = to order food): 뭐 시킬 거예요? = what'll you order?

english: I'll order the bibimbap.
Did you already order?
Yes, I just ordered.
One rice too, please.
grammar: 도 (do = also) replaces 은/는/이/가: 밥도 = rice too.

english: Excuse me, the menu please.
grammar: 저기요 (jeogiyo = excuse me) is the polite way to call restaurant staff.

english: A glass of cola, please.
One whole chicken, please.
grammar: 마리 (mari) counts animals — and whole chickens on menus: 한 마리 (han mari).

english: A bottle of soju, please.
grammar: 병 (byeong = bottle) with native numbers: 한 병 (han byeong = one bottle).

english: Two glasses of beer, please.
This one, please.
grammar: Point and say 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo = this one, please) — orders anything.

english: Cold noodles for me too, please.
We ordered tteokbokki too.
I'll order dumplings as well.
The food came out quickly.
grammar: 나오다 (naoda = to come out) is how Koreans say food arrives: 나왔어요.

english: How does it taste?
grammar: 맛이 어때요? (masi eottaeyo = how's the taste?) — 맛 (mat) = taste.

english: It's really delicious!
This kimchi stew is a bit spicy.
The chili pepper is really spicy.
grammar: 진짜 (jinjja = really) — the casual-but-polite cousin of 정말 (jeongmal).

english: The soup is too salty.
grammar: 너무 (neomu = too) turns praise into complaint: 너무 짜요 = too salty.

english: This cake is too sweet.
Korean fruit is really sweet.
The lemon is so sour.
The broth really hits the spot!
grammar: 시원해요 (siwonhaeyo = refreshing) — Koreans say it even about hot soup that hits the spot.

english: The stew is very hot.
grammar: 뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo) = hot to the touch; spicy-hot is 매워요 (maewoyo).

english: The water is cold.
This side dish is a bit bland.
grammar: 싱거워요 (singgeowoyo = bland) — the opposite of 짜요 (jjayo = salty).

english: The fish is very fresh.
The bread really tastes bad.
grammar: 맛없어요 (madeopseoyo = tastes bad) — 맛 (taste) + 없다 (to not exist).

english: The food at that restaurant wasn't good.
The dessert was too sweet.
The tteokbokki yesterday was really spicy.
The chicken is nice and crispy.
grammar: 치킨 (chikin) means fried chicken only; a live or raw chicken is 닭 (dak).

english: The coffee was too hot.
The cold noodles were so refreshing.
The taste is a little different.
The broth flavor is rich.
Some salt, please.
I don't need sugar.
grammar: 필요 없어요 (piryo eopseoyo = no need) — a polite "I'm good."

english: Ah, I'm full!
grammar: 배불러요 (baebulleoyo = I'm full) — 배 (belly) + 부르다; say it after a good meal.

english: Tonight's dinner is delivery food.
grammar: 배달 (baedal = delivery) — in Korea almost anything arrives at your door.

english: We ordered chicken for delivery.
Last night I had a late-night snack.
grammar: 야식 (yasik = late-night food) — a beloved Korean institution.

english: The delivery is really fast.
The food came thirty minutes later.
grammar: 후에 (hue = after): 삼십 분 후에 = thirty minutes later.

english: I ordered pizza on the app.
Delivery apps are really convenient.
We're going to order Chinese food.
Two bowls of jjajangmyeon, please.
grammar: 그릇 (geureut = bowl) with native numbers: 두 그릇 (du geureut = two bowls).

english: How much is the delivery fee?
grammar: 비 (bi) on the end of a noun = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi = delivery fee).

english: The delivery fee is 3,000 won.
grammar: Money uses Sino numbers: 삼천 원 (samcheon won = 3,000 won).

english: We're waiting for the delivery now.
The food just arrived.
Ramyeon is the best late-night food.
I drank every last drop of the broth.
grammar: 까지 (kkaji = even/up to): 국물까지 = even the broth.

english: Excuse me, the check please.
grammar: 계산서 (gyesanseo = the bill) — ask for it, or just pay at the counter.

english: Do you take cards?
grammar: 돼요? (dwaeyo = does it work?) is the all-purpose "can I...?": 카드 돼요?

english: Yes, cards are fine.
Is cash okay too?
How much did it come to?
grammar: Bills "come out" in Korean: 얼마 나왔어요? (eolma nawasseoyo = how much is it?)

english: It's 40,000 won altogether.
grammar: 만 (man = 10,000) is the money unit: 사만 원 (saman won = 40,000 won).

english: I'll get the bill.
grammar: 계산할게요 (gyesanhalgeyo) — volunteer with -(으)ㄹ게요: 제가 계산할게요 = I've got this.

english: No no, my treat.
grammar: 살게요 (salgeyo) — -(으)ㄹ게요 is the offering form: 제가 살게요 = my treat!

english: Last time Minsu paid.
Today the coffee's on me.
Korea has no tipping.
grammar: No tipping needed in Korea: 팁이 없어요 (tibi eopseoyo).

english: Do you need a receipt?
I'm fine without the receipt.
grammar: 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) politely declines — a soft "no thanks."

english: I got my change.
We split the lunch bill.
grammar: 내다 (naeda = to pay): 같이 냈어요 = we paid together.

english: Yesterday the company paid for dinner.
grammar: 값 (gap = cost) attaches to nouns: 저녁값 (jeonyeokgap = the dinner bill).

english: Was it expensive?
No, it was really cheap.
Yesterday I ate pork belly.
grammar: Past = ㅆ + 어요: 먹었어요 (meogeosseoyo = ate).

english: Last weekend I had galbi.
grammar: 지난 (jinan = last): 지난 주말 (jinan jumal = last weekend).

english: On Friday we ate out as a family.
We had a company dinner yesterday.
grammar: 회식 (hoesik = team dinner) — after-work meals are big in Korean work life.

english: We grilled meat at the company dinner.
grammar: 굽다 (gupda = to grill) → 구워요 (guwoyo) — you grill at the table in Korea.

english: What did you have for lunch?
I had kimchi fried rice.
I tried soft-tofu stew for the first time.
It was really delicious.
I ate way too much.
My stomach hurt.
So I skipped dinner.
grammar: 그래서 (geuraeseo = so/therefore) links a cause to what happened.

english: What are you going to eat tonight?
grammar: Future = -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 먹을 거예요 (meogeul geoyeyo = will eat).

english: I'm going to make bulgogi.
Tomorrow I'm having lunch with a friend.
This weekend we'll try a new restaurant.
grammar: 새 (sae = new) sits before a noun: 새 식당 = a new restaurant.

english: We'll have green-onion pancake there.
grammar: 파전 (pajeon = green-onion pancake) — Korea's favorite rainy-day food.

english: We'll drink makgeolli too.
Tomorrow I'll have breakfast at home.
Next week I'm going to learn to cook.
Mom is going to make seaweed soup.
grammar: 미역국 (miyeokguk = seaweed soup) — the traditional Korean birthday breakfast.

english: We'll have cake on the birthday too.
Guests are coming this evening.
So I'll prepare lots of food.
Do you take the subway to work?
grammar: 로 (ro = by) marks transport: 지하철로 (jihacheollo = by subway).

english: Yes, I ride the subway every day.
Which line do you take?
grammar: 호선 (hoseon = subway line) takes Sino numbers: 2호선 (i-hoseon = Line 2).

english: I take Line 2.
I get off at City Hall Station.
grammar: 내리다 (naerida = to get off): 역에서 내려요 = get off at the station.

english: I'll get off at the next station.
Where do you transfer?
grammar: 갈아타요 (garatayo = transfer), from 갈아타다 — 갈아 (change) + 타다 (ride).

english: I transfer at Gangnam Station.
From here you take Line 3.
Do you have a T-money card?
grammar: 티머니 (T-money) — the tap card for subway, bus, and even taxis.

english: I top up my T-money at the convenience store.
grammar: 충전하다 (chungjeonhada = to top up/charge) — cards and phone batteries alike.

english: Yesterday I loaded 10,000 won onto it.
The subway is faster than the bus.
grammar: 보다 (boda) after a noun = than: 버스보다 빨라요 = faster than the bus.

english: At rush hour there are so many people.
grammar: 출근 (chulgeun = going to work): 출근 시간 = rush hour.

english: Is there a subway station around here?
What time is the last train?
grammar: 막차 (makcha = last train) — miss it and it's a taxi night.

english: I missed the last train.
So I took a taxi.
I listen to music on the subway.
How many stops is it?
grammar: 정거장 (jeonggeojang) counts stops: 세 정거장 (se jeonggeojang = three stops).

english: It's three stops.
Where is the bus stop?
Which bus do you take?
grammar: 번 (beon = number) takes Sino numbers: 273번 버스 = bus number 273.

english: I take bus number 273.
Does this bus go to City Hall?
The bus is coming now.
I missed the bus this morning.
The next bus comes in ten minutes.
grammar: 분 (bun = minute) takes Sino numbers: 10분 (sip bun = ten minutes).

english: The bus was way too crowded.
There were no seats.
I got off the bus.
I waited five minutes at the stop.
How much is the bus fare?
grammar: 요금 (yogeum = fare) — bus, subway, and taxi all use this word.

english: It's 1,500 won.
You tap your card here.
grammar: 찍다 (jjikda = to tap/stamp): 카드를 찍어요 = tap your card.

english: You tap your card on the bus too.
I'm going to catch a taxi.
grammar: 잡다 (japda = to catch): 택시를 잡아요 = hail a taxi.

english: I called a taxi with the app.
The taxi is coming soon.
Is the fare to the airport expensive?
What's the base fare?
Traffic is really bad.
grammar: 막히다 (makida = to be blocked): 길이 막혀요 = the roads are jammed.

english: Yesterday traffic was terrible.
Driver, I'll get out here.
grammar: 내릴게요 (naerilgeyo) — -(으)ㄹ게요 signals an action for the listener: 여기서 내릴게요 = I'll get off here.

english: The fare came to 20,000 won.
I paid by card.
Taxis cost more at night.
The subway is cheaper than a taxi.
Next month I'm going to Busan.
grammar: 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) — 달 (moon) also means month.

english: I booked KTX tickets.
grammar: 예매하다 (yemaehada = to book ahead) — train, movie, and concert tickets.

english: I'm going from Seoul to Busan by train.
grammar: 에서...까지 (eseo...kkaji) = from...to: 서울에서 부산까지.

english: KTX tickets are a bit pricey.
I really love train travel.
We'll meet at Seoul Station.
I ate a boxed lunch on the train.
grammar: 도시락 (dosirak = boxed lunch) — a classic of Korean train rides.

english: The tickets are already sold out.
grammar: 매진 (maejin = sold out): 매진이에요 — you'll see it on booking screens.

english: So I bought a bus ticket.
The express bus is comfortable too.
I bought snacks at the rest stop.
grammar: 휴게소 (hyugeso = highway rest stop) — its snacks are a road-trip ritual.

english: The next train leaves at two.
grammar: 시 (si = o'clock) takes native numbers: 두 시 (du si = two o'clock).

english: The train just left.
We'll arrive at six in the evening.
Where is the platform?
grammar: 승강장 (seunggangjang = platform) — signs also say 타는 곳 (taneun got).

english: I got lost.
grammar: 길을 잃어버렸어요 (gireul ireobeoryeosseoyo = I lost my way) — the traveler's essential.

english: Excuse me, where is Myeongdong?
Is it far from here?
No, it's very close.
You go right from here.
grammar: (으)로 marks direction: 오른쪽으로 (oreunjjogeuro = to the right).

english: Turn left at the intersection.
grammar: 사거리 (sageori = intersection) — 사 (four) + 거리 (street): where four roads meet.

english: Go straight ahead.
grammar: 쭉 (jjuk = straight on): 쭉 가요 — usually with a hand pointing the way.

english: Cross the street in front of the bank.
It's next to the convenience store.
It's across from the cafe.
grammar: 건너편 (geonneopyeon = the far side): 카페 건너편 = across from the cafe.

english: Which exit is it?
grammar: Subway exits are numbered: 4번 출구 (sabeon chulgu = exit 4) — how Koreans set meeting spots.

english: Let's meet at exit 4.
I check the map app.
I found the station on the map.
Wait at the traffic light.
I crossed at the crosswalk.
I don't know the way.
I asked a subway staff member.
grammar: 물어보다 (mureoboda = to ask): 길을 물어봤어요 = asked the way.

english: My friend sent me a map.
Now I know the way.
grammar: 이제 (ije = now, from now on) — for a change of state: 이제 알아요 = now I know.

english: How long does it take to your office?
grammar: 얼마나 걸려요? (eolmana geollyeoyo = how long does it take?) — THE commute question.

english: Forty minutes by subway.
How long from here to the airport?
It takes almost two hours.
How long did it take?
It took thirty minutes.
grammar: Sino numbers stack: 삼십 (samsip = thirty) = 삼 (3) × 십 (10).

english: It took longer than I expected.
grammar: 생각보다 (saenggakboda = than expected): 생각보다 오래 = longer than expected.

english: Today there was no traffic.
So I arrived early.
It takes an hour by plane.
grammar: 시간 (sigan = hours of duration) takes native numbers: 한 시간 (han sigan).

english: We fly to Jeju Island.
grammar: 제주도 (Jejudo) — Korea's holiday island; Seoul–Jeju is the world's busiest air route.

english: I got to the airport two hours early.
It's a short trip from home to work.
Last year I traveled around Korea.
I saw the sea in Busan.
Haeundae was wonderful.
I went to Gyeongju by train.
I took lots of photos there.
grammar: 사진을 찍다 (sajineul jjikda = to take a photo) — same 찍다 as tapping a card!

english: The hotel was close to the station.
Last summer I went to Jeju.
I walked along the beach.
We traveled by rental car.
grammar: 렌터카 (renteoka = rental car) — Konglish, straight from "rent-a-car".

english: The trip was too short.
The weather was really lovely.
I bought souvenirs at the market.
I sent the trip photos to my family.
grammar: 한테 (hante = to a person): 가족한테 보냈어요 = sent to my family.

english: I still can't forget that trip.
grammar: 못 (mot = can't) before the verb: 못 잊어요 = can't forget.

english: I'll go again next year.
Next week I'm going on a trip.
grammar: 여행을 가다 (yeohaengeul gada = to go on a trip) — trips are "gone", not "made".

english: Where will you go?
I'm going to Gangneung with a friend.
We'll book a hotel near the sea.
grammar: 예약 (yeyak) reserves places; 예매 (yemae) books tickets.

english: I'll buy the train tickets in advance.
I'll get my suitcase ready.
On Jeju we'll go to Hallasan.
grammar: 산 (san = mountain): 한라산 (Hallasan) — Korea's tallest, on Jeju.

english: We'll look around downtown Seoul.
grammar: 구경하다 (gugyeonghada = to sightsee/look around) — markets, palaces, anything.

english: We'll also see Gyeongbokgung Palace.
We're going to wear hanbok.
grammar: Wear a 한복 (hanbok = traditional dress) and palace entry in Seoul is free.

english: We'll have dinner at the night market.
Where will you go on vacation?
grammar: 때 (ttae = the time of): 휴가 때 (hyuga ttae = during vacation).

english: I'm going to travel around Europe.
I'm going to make a travel plan.
grammar: Plans are "built" in Korean: 계획을 세워요 (gyehoegeul sewoyo = make a plan).

english: I'm going to the market with a friend today.
grammar: 랑 (rang) = 'with/and' after a vowel: 친구랑 (chingu-rang = with a friend).

english: I buy fruit and vegetables at the market.
grammar: 이랑 (irang) = 'and/with' after a consonant: 과일이랑 야채 (gwail-irang yachae); after a vowel it's 랑 (rang).

english: The supermarket is close to my house.
The convenience store is open 24 hours.
I look around at the department store.
grammar: 구경해요 (gugyeonghaeyo) = look around, browse — shopping without buying.

english: This store sells clothes.
grammar: 팔다 (palda) = to sell: 옷을 팔아요 (os-eul parayo = sells clothes). To buy = 사다 (sada).

english: I buy milk at the convenience store.
The market is cheaper than the supermarket.
grammar: N보다 (boda) = 'than N': 마트보다 싸요 (mateu-boda ssayo = cheaper than the supermarket).

english: On weekends the department store is crowded.
grammar: 많다 (manta) = to be many: 사람이 많아요 (saram-i manayo = it's crowded).

english: Where is a clothing store?
This market is famous for its fish.
The store opens at ten in the morning.
The supermarket closes at ten at night.
I buy ramyeon and gimbap at the convenience store.
There's a new store over there.
grammar: 새 (sae) = 'new' before a noun: 새 가게 (sae gage = a new store).

english: How much is this bag?
How much is that hat?
This book is 10,000 won.
grammar: Prices use Sino numbers + 원 (won): 만 원 (man won = 10,000 won).

english: The coffee is 4,000 won.
These shoes are 50,000 won.
grammar: 오만 (oman) = 50,000: 오 (o = five) times 만 (man = ten thousand).

english: The gimbap here is 2,000 won.
The water is 500 won.
grammar: 오백 (obaek) = 500: 오 (o = five) + 백 (baek = hundred).

english: This umbrella is 9,000 won.
That bag is 20,000 won.
Five apples are 5,000 won.
grammar: 개 (gae) counts things with NATIVE numbers: 다섯 개 (daseot gae = five items).

english: The T-shirt is 15,000 won.
grammar: 만 오천 (man ocheon) = 15,000 — stack 만 (10,000) + 오천 (5,000).

english: This watch is too expensive.
Please give me a little discount.
grammar: 깎아 주세요 (kkakka juseyo) = 'please lower the price' — fine at markets, not at malls.

english: At the market, people haggle over prices.
The price is a bit expensive.
grammar: 좀 (jom) softens statements: 좀 비싸요 (jom bissayo = it's a bit expensive).

english: This fruit is really cheap.
Is it on sale now?
grammar: 세일 (seil) = sale, from English; 세일해요 (seilhaeyo) = it's on sale.

english: The department store is having a sale now.
The sale price is 30,000 won.
These clothes are on sale.
grammar: N 중이에요 (jung-ieyo) = 'in the middle of N': 세일 중이에요 (seil jung-ieyo = it's on sale).

english: Today only, it's 5,000 won.
grammar: 만 (man) after a noun = 'only': 오늘만 (oneul-man = today only) — same sound as 만 = 10,000!

english: How much was that?
grammar: 였어요 (yeosseoyo) = 'was' after a vowel: 얼마였어요? (eolma-yeosseoyo = how much was it?)

english: It was a bit expensive.
grammar: Past adds ㅆ: 비싸요 → 비쌌어요 (bissasseoyo = was expensive).

english: Yesterday it was cheaper.
grammar: 더 (deo) = more: 더 쌌어요 (deo ssasseoyo = was cheaper).

english: I spent too much money.
grammar: 쓰다 (sseuda) = write, use, AND spend: 돈을 썼어요 (don-eul sseosseoyo = spent money).

english: What color do you like?
grammar: 색 (saek) = color: 무슨 색 (museun saek = what color).

english: I like blue.
grammar: Color words end in -색 (saek): 파란색 (paransaek = blue).

english: The red skirt is pretty.
grammar: 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (yeppeoyo = is pretty): the ㅡ drops before 어요.

english: I often wear black pants.
I need a white T-shirt.
Do you have a yellow umbrella?
How about the green hat?
Do you have a different color?
grammar: 다른 (dareun) = another/different before a noun: 다른 색 (dareun saek = a different color).

english: This color is really pretty.
I'm buying a skirt and pants.
That T-shirt has a pretty color.
I often wear a hat.
grammar: 쓰다 also = wear on your head: 모자를 써요 (moja-reul sseoyo = I wear a hat).

english: I bought new glasses.
grammar: 새로 (saero) = newly, anew: 새로 샀어요 (saero sasseoyo = newly bought).

english: How about this dress?
I buy socks at the market.
Those dress shoes are expensive.
I'm looking for winter clothes.
There are many summer skirts.
These clothes are really light.
grammar: ㅂ-verbs soften: 가볍다 → 가벼워요 (gabyeowoyo = is light).

english: That bag is heavy.
The blue sneakers are stylish.
Red doesn't suit me.
grammar: 어울리다 = to suit: 저한테 어울려요 (jeohante eoullyeoyo = it suits me).

english: How much are these gloves?
I'm buying a scarf as a present.
grammar: 선물 (seonmul) = present, gift: 선물로 (seonmul-lo = as a gift).

english: This clothing store has cheap T-shirts.
Try this skirt on.
grammar: V-어 봐요 = 'try V-ing': 입어 봐요 (ibeo bwayo = try it on). 봐요 works as its own helper word.

english: Try the shoes on.
grammar: 신다 (sinda) = wear on your FEET: 신발을 신어요 (sinbal-eul sineoyo = wear shoes).

english: Try this hat on.
I tried on pants at the store.
grammar: 봐요 → 봤어요 (bwasseoyo): 입어 봤어요 (ibeo bwasseoyo = tried it on).

english: What size do you wear?
grammar: 몇 (myeot) asks 'what number': 몇 사이즈 (myeot saijeu = what size).

english: This size is too small for me.
grammar: 한테 (hante) = 'to/for (a person)': 저한테 작아요 (jeohante jagayo = small for me).

english: Do you have another size?
These pants are a bit big.
The shoes are a little small.
grammar: 조금 (jogeum) = a little; 좀 (jom) is its casual short form.

english: This T-shirt fits.
grammar: 맞다 (matda) = to fit, be right: 사이즈가 맞아요 (saijeu-ga majayo = the size fits).

english: Did those clothes fit well?
This hat suits you well.
The dress suited you really well.
Where is the mirror?
The fitting room is over there.
Give it a try on.
grammar: 한번 (hanbeon) softens suggestions: 한번 입어 봐요 (hanbeon ibeo bwayo = just try it on).

english: I tried on these dress shoes.
The skirt is too long.
grammar: 길다 (gilda) = to be long: 치마가 길어요 (chima-ga gireoyo = the skirt is long).

english: The pants are a little short.
grammar: 짧다 (jjalda) = to be short: 바지가 짧아요 (baji-ga jjalbayo = the pants are short).

english: This coat is warm.
We don't have that size right now.
These shoes are comfortable on the feet.
grammar: 편하다 (pyeonhada) = comfortable: 발이 편해요 (bar-i pyeonhaeyo = easy on the feet).

english: Ma'am/Sir, how about this color?
grammar: 손님 (sonnim) = guest, customer — how shop staff politely address you.

english: Sorry, those clothes are not on sale.
These sneakers are more comfortable.
I pay by card.
grammar: N(으)로 = 'by, with': 카드로 계산해요 (kadeu-ro gyesanhaeyo = pay by card).

english: Do you have cash?
grammar: 현금 (hyeongeum) = cash; 카드 (kadeu) = card — the checkout question pair.

english: Please give me the receipt too.
Here is the receipt.
Can I get a refund?
grammar: 돼요 (dwaeyo) = 'it's possible': 환불이 돼요? (hwanbur-i dwaeyo? = is a refund possible?)

english: I got a refund for these clothes.
grammar: 환불 (hwanbul) = refund; 환불해요 (hwanbulhaeyo) = get or give a refund.

english: I'm exchanging the size.
grammar: 바꾸다 → 바꿔요 (bakkwoyo = exchange, change): 우 + 어 contracts to 워.

target: 이 바지를 다른 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요.
english: Please exchange these pants for a different size.
grammar: V-어 주세요 = 'please do it for me': 바꿔 주세요 (bakkwo juseyo = please exchange it).

english: I exchanged that bag yesterday.
Do you need a bag?
grammar: 봉투 (bongtu) = shopping bag, envelope — cashiers ask 봉투가 필요해요?

english: Yes, one bag please.
grammar: 하나 (hana) = one, standing alone; before a counter it becomes 한 (han).

english: The clerk is really kind.
grammar: 점원 (jeomwon) = store clerk; 친절해요 (chinjeolhaeyo) = is kind.

english: Ask the clerk over there.
grammar: 물어봐요 (mureobwayo) = ask (and see) — 봐요 again as a helper.

english: The card doesn't work.
Thank you. I'll come again.
grammar: 또 (tto) = again: 또 올 거예요 (tto ol geoyeyo = I'll come again).

english: Yesterday I bought fruit at the market.
grammar: Past = ㅆ + 어요: 사요 → 샀어요 (sasseoyo = bought).

english: Last weekend I went to the department store.
grammar: 지난 (jinan) = last, past: 지난 주말 (jinan jumal = last weekend).

english: I bought two skirts there.
grammar: 벌 (beol) counts clothes: 치마 두 벌 (chima du beol = two skirts).

english: I bought a pair of shoes.
grammar: 켤레 (kyeolle) counts pairs of shoes: 한 켤레 (han kyeolle = one pair).

english: I bought a birthday present.
Yesterday I spent a lot of money.
grammar: 많이 (mani) = a lot: 많이 썼어요 (mani sseosseoyo = spent a lot).

english: I bought that watch on sale.
grammar: 때 (ttae) = 'the time of': 세일 때 (seil ttae = during the sale).

english: Last week I bought this coat.
grammar: 지난주 (jinanju) = last week — one word, no space.

english: I haggled the price down at the market.
My friend received the present.
grammar: 받다 (batda) = to receive: 선물을 받았어요 (seonmur-eul badasseoyo = received a gift).

english: Tomorrow I'll go to the supermarket.
grammar: Future = stem + ㄹ 거예요: 가다 → 갈 거예요 (gal geoyeyo = will go).

english: This weekend I'll buy new clothes.
grammar: 살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) = will buy — from 사다 (sada), not 살다 (salda = live)!

english: Next week I'll go to the market.
grammar: 다음 (daeum) = next: 다음 주 (daeum ju = next week).

english: I'll buy a birthday present for my friend.
I'll look around at the department store.
I'll try this dress on.
grammar: 볼 거예요 (bol geoyeyo) = will see, will try: 입어 볼 거예요 (ibeo bol geoyeyo = will try it on).

english: I'll spend only a little money.
I'll buy sneakers in the sale.
When will you go shopping?
Next month I'll exchange the bag.
grammar: 달 (dal) = month (and moon): 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month).

english: Our family is five people.
grammar: 우리 (uri = our) is how Koreans say 'my' for family: 우리 가족 (uri gajok = my family).

english: Do you have a family photo?
My parents are in Seoul.
grammar: 계세요 (gyeseyo) = honorific 'are (there)' for parents and elders; the plain form is 있어요 (isseoyo).

english: My older brother works at a company.
My husband cooks well.
grammar: 잘 + verb = do well: 요리를 잘해요 (yori-reul jalhaeyo = cooks well).

english: I have an older sister.
grammar: 언니 (eonni) = older sister for a FEMALE speaker. Men say 누나 (nuna).

english: My older sister is three years older than me.
Minsu has an older sister.
grammar: 누나 (nuna) = older sister for a MALE speaker — 민수 (a man) says 누나.

target: 준호 씨는 형이 두 명 있어요.
english: Junho has two older brothers.
grammar: 형 (hyeong) = older brother for a MALE speaker. Women say 오빠 (oppa).

english: Sujin has an older brother.
grammar: 오빠 (oppa) = older brother for a FEMALE speaker — 수진 (a woman) says 오빠.

english: I have one younger brother.
grammar: 동생 = younger sibling: 남동생 (namdongsaeng = brother), 여동생 (yeodongsaeng = sister).

english: My younger sister is a university student.
My younger sibling is at school now.
My grandmother is in Busan.
grammar: 계세요 (gyeseyo) = honorific 'is (there)' for elders; the plain form is 있어요 (isseoyo).

english: My grandfather is at home now.
Grandma, please have some cake.
grammar: 드세요 (deuseyo) = honorific 'please eat' for elders; the plain form is 먹어요 (meogeoyo).

english: My grandfather is eating breakfast.
grammar: 드세요 also STATES what an elder does: 아침을 드세요 (achim-eul deuseyo = he's eating breakfast).

english: My aunt lives in America.
grammar: 이모 (imo) = aunt on Mom's side — Korean kinship words mark the exact relation.

english: My uncle cooks really well.
I have three cousins.
grammar: 사촌 (sachon) = cousin — literally 'four degrees' of kinship distance.

english: We also have a puppy at home.
Do you have a son?
I have one daughter.
My husband works at a bank.
My wife is a teacher.
grammar: 아내 (anae) = my wife; another person's wife is politely 부인 (buin).

english: The baby is really cute.
My older sister is married.
grammar: 결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) — Korean uses past 'got married' for 'is married'.

english: My older brother is still a student.
grammar: 형 (hyeong) = a man's older brother, so this speaker is male. Women say 오빠 (oppa).

english: My older brother got married last week.
grammar: 오빠 (oppa) = a woman's older brother, so this speaker is female. Men say 형 (hyeong).

english: I live with my parents.
grammar: 이랑 (irang) = 'with' after a consonant: 부모님이랑 (bumonim-irang = with my parents).

english: My older sister works at a hospital.
grammar: 누나 (nuna) = a man's older sister, so this speaker is male. Women say 언니 (eonni).

english: My whole family is in Seoul.
I talk on the phone with my younger sister every day.
My family cooks together on weekends.
I meet my family on Sunday.
My older sister is tall.
grammar: 키가 커요 (ki-ga keoyo) = 'is tall' — literally 'height is big'.

english: My younger brother is short.
My younger brother has short hair.
grammar: 머리 (meori) = head AND hair: 머리가 짧아요 (meori-ga jjalbayo = has short hair).

english: My younger sister has long hair.
My younger sibling has big eyes.
The baby's hands are really small.
My older brother wears glasses.
grammar: 쓰다 also covers glasses: 안경을 써요 (angyeong-eul sseoyo = wears glasses).

english: I wear glasses too.
That actor has a small face.
grammar: Koreans compliment 얼굴이 작아요 (eolgur-i jagayo = 'your face is small') — it means good-looking!

english: Sujin is really pretty.
Junho is cool.
Our puppy is so cute.
Minsu is kind.
Jieun is very smart.
My friend is really funny.
My friend is warm-hearted.
grammar: 마음이 따뜻해요 (maeum-i ttatteuthaeyo) = warm-hearted — 마음 = heart, mind.

english: My younger sibling has a nice personality.
My son has a loud voice.
I look like my dad.
grammar: 닮았어요 (dalmasseoyo) = resemble — always in the past form: 아빠를 닮았어요 (I take after Dad).

english: My younger sister looks like Mom.
My older brother and I look really alike.
Where is that person right now?
grammar: 그분 (geubun) = respectful 'that person' — pair it with polite verbs like 계세요 (gyeseyo).

english: That person is still young.
grammar: 아직 (ajik) = still, yet: 아직 젊어요 (ajik jeolmeoyo = still young).

english: My uncle is strong.
grammar: 세다 (seda) = to be strong: 힘이 세요 (him-i seyo = is strong).

english: My older sister's hair is brown.
My eyes are brown.
Minsu has a nice voice.
That child is really sweet.
grammar: 착해요 (chakaeyo) = kind-hearted, well-behaved — the go-to praise for kids.

english: My daughter laughs often.
My son is good at sports.
Jieun sings well.
My cousin is the same age as me.
grammar: 같아요 (gatayo) = is the same: 나이가 같아요 (nai-ga gatayo = same age).

english: I don't know that person's name.
I know the face.
How tall are you?
How old are you?
grammar: 살 (sal) counts age with native numbers: 몇 살이에요? (myeot sar-ieyo? = how old are you?)

english: I am twenty years old.
grammar: 스무 (seumu) = twenty before a counter: 스무 살 (seumu sal = 20 years old).

english: My younger sibling is eight years old.
grammar: 여덟 (yeodeol) = eight (native number): 여덟 살 (yeodeol sal = eight years old).

english: My older sister is thirty.
Our baby is two years old.
Our dog is old.
grammar: 나이가 많아요 (nai-ga manayo) = 'is old' — literally 'age is many'.

english: How old are you, if I may ask?
grammar: 나이가 어떻게 돼요? (nai-ga eotteoke dwaeyo?) = polite 'how old are you?' — softer than 몇 살이에요?

english: Minsu, when is your birthday?
Today is my birthday.
Happy birthday!
grammar: 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukahaeyo) = happy birthday — literally 'I congratulate your birthday'.

english: Tomorrow is Mom's birthday.
Dad's birthday is next week.
We're having a birthday party.
There's a birthday party on Saturday.
I'm inviting friends to the party.
grammar: -들 (deul) makes plurals: 친구들 (chingu-deul = friends). Korean often skips it.

english: I invited my older sister to the party.
I got a book as a birthday present.
We eat the cake together.
My friend made the cake.
I wrote a birthday card.
What present would be good?
My friends are singing a song.
grammar: 부르다 → 불러요 (bulleoyo = sing, call): 르-verbs double the ㄹ.

english: I turn thirty next month.
I got a watch on my birthday last year.
I'll have a party on my birthday next year.
How do you do?
grammar: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (cheoeum boepgetseumnida) = formal 'nice to meet you' — 합니다체, for first meetings.

english: It's really nice to meet you.
What is your name, please?
My name is Jieun.
This is my husband.
grammar: 이쪽은 (ijjog-eun) = 'this side is…' — the polite-neutral way to introduce family and friends.

english: I'm introducing my friend to my family.
This is my mother.
grammar: 이분 takes polite 세요: 어머니세요 (eomeoni-seyo = is my mother); the plain form is 어머니예요.

english: Today I'm introducing my father to my friend.
This is my younger sibling.
grammar: 이쪽은 (ijjog-eun) = 'this side is...' — a natural way to introduce someone.

english: Where are you from?
grammar: 왔어요 (wasseoyo) = came: 어디에서 왔어요? (eodieseo wasseoyo? = where are you from?)

english: I'm from America.
Are you from Canada?
When did you come to Korea?
What work do you do?
Where do you live now?
How are you doing?
grammar: 잘 지내요? (jal jinaeyo?) = 'how are you?' — literally 'are you getting along well?'

english: Yes, I'm doing well.
Did you have a good weekend?
It's been such a long time!
grammar: 오랜만이에요 (oraenman-ieyo) = 'long time no see' — literally 'it's been a while'.

english: Minsu, long time no see!
Is it your first time here?
grammar: 처음 (cheoeum) = first time: 처음이에요 (cheoeum-ieyo = it's my first time).

english: It's my first time in Korea.
What's your phone number?
Let's have coffee together tomorrow.
grammar: 해요체 doubles as 'let's': 같이 마셔요 (gachi masyeoyo = let's drink together).

english: See you again next time.
Do you have a business card?
Here's my business card.
I've heard a lot about you.
grammar: 말씀 많이 들었어요 (malsseum mani deureosseoyo) = 'I've heard a lot about you' — a warm meeting phrase.

english: Do you come here often?
I'll introduce my family this weekend.
I go to the office every morning.
I get up at seven in the morning.
grammar: 시 hours take native numbers: 일곱 시 (ilgop si = 7 o'clock).

english: I leave the house at eight.
I commute to work by subway.
grammar: 출근해요 (chulgeunhaeyo) = go to work; (으)로 = by: 지하철로 = by subway.

english: I transfer from the bus to the subway.
grammar: 갈아타요 (garatayo) = transfer — literally 'change-ride.'

english: It takes forty minutes to the office.
grammar: 분 minutes take Sino numbers: 사십 분 (sasip bun = 40 minutes).

english: There are so many people on the morning subway.
I missed the bus this morning.
grammar: 놓쳤어요 (nochyeosseoyo) = missed it — buses, trains, chances.

english: So I was a little late to work.
Tomorrow I'll leave earlier.
I wait for the bus at the stop.
I walk ten minutes to the subway station.
In the morning I listen to music on the subway.
The traffic is really bad today.
grammar: 길이 막혀요 (giri makyeoyo) = 'the road is blocked' — Korean for a traffic jam.

english: What time do you go to work?
I get to work by nine.
The office is close to my house.
The roads are crowded at rush hour.
grammar: 퇴근 시간 (toegeun sigan) = 'leaving-work time' = the evening rush hour.

english: Yesterday I came home by taxi.
From next week I'll bike to work.
grammar: 부터 (buteo) = from/starting: 다음 주부터 = from next week.

english: I buy coffee on the way to work.
grammar: 출근길 (chulgeungil) = the way to work; -길 (gil) makes 'route' words.

english: I read the news on the subway.
The bus came late today.
There's a cafe in front of the office.
I exercise before work.
Our company is in Seoul.
grammar: 우리 (uri) = our — Koreans say 'our company,' 'our family,' even 'our house.'

english: I work in an office.
My colleagues are really kind.
grammar: 동료 (dongnyo) = colleague; -들 (deul) makes it plural.

english: Hello, Manager Kim.
grammar: At work use title + 님: 과장님 (gwajangnim = manager) — never the bare name!

english: The department head is on a business trip now.
grammar: 부장님 (bujangnim) = department head; add -세요 for respect: 출장 중이세요 (chuljang jungiseyo = is away on a trip).

english: I had lunch with the team leader.
grammar: 팀장님 (timjangnim) = team leader — 팀 (tim) comes from English 'team.'

english: The boss is in a meeting right now.
grammar: -세요 adds respect for the boss: 회의 중이세요 (hoeui jungiseyo = is in a meeting).

english: A new colleague is coming next week.
I work on the marketing team.
The office is quiet today.
The computer suddenly isn't working.
grammar: 안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) = it doesn't work — an everyday essential phrase.

english: The printer is broken again.
grammar: 고장이에요 (gojangieyo) = it's broken; 또 (tto) = again.

english: I check my email in the morning.
I sent the report to the department head.
grammar: 께 (kke) = honorific 'to' for superiors/elders: 부장님께 (bujangnimkke); 한테 is the plain everyday form.

english: I put the documents on the desk.
My colleague isn't at her desk today.
Lunchtime is at twelve.
I eat lunch at the company cafeteria.
I drink coffee with a colleague.
grammar: 랑 (rang) = with/and, casual: 동료랑 (dongnyorang = with a colleague).

english: There's even more work in the afternoon.
The work isn't finished yet.
I have so much to do today.
grammar: 할 일 (hal il) = things to do — 할 turns 하다 into 'to-do.'

english: On Friday afternoons I feel good.
Monday mornings are always hard.
grammar: 힘들어요 (himdeureoyo) = it's tough — for effort and energy, not taste.

english: I work at a bank.
grammar: 다녀요 (danyeoyo) = go regularly — Korean's verb for attending work or school.

english: My older sister works at the same company too.
How's work these days?
I'm getting a lot of stress these days.
grammar: 스트레스를 받아요 (seuteureseureul badayo) = 'receive stress' = to be stressed.

english: There's a meeting at ten.
Where is the meeting room?
grammar: -실 (sil) = room: 회의실 (hoeuisil) = meeting room, 화장실 = bathroom.

english: The meeting took two hours.
I'm preparing for tomorrow's meeting.
I'm making the presentation materials.
grammar: 발표 (balpyo) = presentation; 자료 (jaryo) = materials.

english: There's an important presentation next week.
I presented at the meeting.
The presentation went well.
I got a lot of questions at the meeting.
Today's meeting was too long.

target: 오후 세 시에 팀 회의가 있어요.
english: There's a team meeting at three p.m.
I prepared coffee before the meeting.
We'll have lunch after the meeting.
grammar: 후에 (hue) = after: 회의 후에 (hoeui hue = after the meeting).

english: I took notes in the meeting.
I'm sending the report by Friday.
One more task came up.
grammar: 생겼어요 (saenggyeosseoyo) = came up/appeared — new things happening.

english: Today I'm organizing documents.
We start the project next month.
The deadline is tomorrow.
grammar: 마감 (magam) = deadline — you'll hear it constantly in Korean offices.

english: We have a company dinner tonight.
grammar: 회식 (hoesik) = after-work team dinner — a big part of Korean office life.

english: We ate pork belly at the company dinner.
grammar: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal) = grilled pork belly — the classic team-dinner menu.

english: The company is paying for dinner.
grammar: 내요 (naeyo) = pays: 회사가 내요 = the company pays.

english: After the dinner we went to karaoke.
grammar: 노래방 (noraebang) = karaoke room — round two of many team dinners.

english: Yesterday's company dinner ended late.
What are you going to eat for lunch?
I ate kimchi stew with my colleagues.
grammar: 김치찌개 (kimchijjigae) = kimchi stew — a lunch-menu regular.

english: Today's lunch is on me.
grammar: 제가 사요 (jega sayo) = 'I'm buying' — how you offer to treat.

english: A junior colleague bought the coffee.
grammar: 후배 (hubae) = your junior at work or school; your senior = 선배 (seonbae).

target: 식사 후에 다 같이 카페에 가요.
english: After the meal we all go to a cafe.
On Fridays we have chicken and beer.
grammar: 치킨에 맥주 = chicken paired with beer (에 links food combos); the whole set takes 먹어요, hence 치맥 (chimaek).

english: The day after a company dinner I'm always tired.
When is the next company dinner?
I like company dinners.
We had birthday cake at the office.
I'm working late again today.
grammar: 야근 (yageun) = working overtime into the night — common office Korean.

english: Yesterday I worked overtime until ten.

target: 이번 주에 야근을 세 번 했어요.
english: I worked late three times this week.
grammar: 번 (beon) counts times, with native numbers: 세 번 (se beon = three times).

english: After overtime I went home by taxi.
I won't work late tomorrow.
It's hard because there's so much work.
grammar: -아서/어서 = because: 많아서 (manaseo = because there's a lot).

english: I'm busy every day these days.
Last week I was really busy.
Next week won't be busy.
There's not much work today.
grammar: 별로 (byeollo) + negative = not really: 별로 없어요 = not much.

english: I leave work right at six.
grammar: 퇴근해요 (toegeunhaeyo) = leave work — the opposite of 출근 (chulgeun).

english: Yesterday I left work early.
A colleague is still at the office.
Tomorrow is payday!
grammar: 월급 (wolgeup) = monthly salary; 월급날 (wolgeumnal — ㅂ+ㄴ sounds like ㅁㄴ) = payday.

english: I got this month's salary.
What will you do with your salary?
My salary went up a little.
grammar: 올랐어요 (ollasseoyo) = went up — salaries, prices, temperatures.

english: I like my job.
I'm looking for a new job these days.
From next month I'll be at a new company.
I really need a vacation.
grammar: 휴가 (hyuga) = vacation/leave from work.

english: On weekdays I get up at six thirty.
grammar: 평일 (pyeongil) = weekday; 반 (ban) = half past.

english: In the morning I shower and get dressed.
grammar: -고 (go) links actions in order: 샤워하고 (syawohago = shower and then).

english: I usually eat breakfast at home.
I drink two cups of coffee a day.
Yesterday morning I got up late.
So I couldn't eat breakfast.
grammar: 못 (mot) = can't/couldn't manage: 못 먹었어요 = couldn't eat.

english: Tomorrow I'll get up at six.
After lunch I take a short walk.
I get home at seven in the evening.
In the evening I eat with my family.
At night I watch Korean dramas.
I usually go to bed at eleven.
Good work again today.
grammar: 수고했어요 (sugohaesseoyo) = 'you worked hard' — the everyday office goodbye.

english: I'm off first. See you tomorrow!
grammar: 저 먼저 가요 (jeo meonjeo gayo) — the polite 'I'm leaving first' at the office.

english: On Wednesday I go to Busan on a business trip.
grammar: 출장 (chuljang) = business trip: 출장을 가요 = go on a business trip.

english: I came back from the business trip yesterday.

target: 다음 주 금요일에 휴가를 쓸 거예요.
english: I'll use a vacation day next Friday.
grammar: 휴가를 써요 (hyugareul sseoyo) = 'use' vacation days — 쓰다 means write AND use.

english: I live in an apartment.
grammar: Most city Koreans live in 아파트 (apateu) — big high-rise complexes.

english: Our place is on the fifteenth floor.
grammar: 층 (cheung) = floor, with Sino numbers: 십오 층 (sibo cheung = 15th floor).

english: I can see the mountains from home.
The living room is very spacious.
grammar: 거실 (geosil) = living room; 넓어요 (neolbeoyo) = is spacious.

english: I cook in the kitchen.
There are two rooms.
grammar: 개 (gae) = general counter, native numbers: 두 개 (du gae = two things).

english: The bathroom is a bit small.
There are lots of plant pots on the balcony.
grammar: 베란다 (beranda) = balcony — where Koreans keep plants and laundry.

english: The elevator is broken again.
The people next door are kind.
In the morning I open all the windows.
There's a park near my house.
The mart is right next to the subway station.
I moved last month.
grammar: 이사해요 (isahaeyo) = move house; 지난달 (jinandal) = last month.

english: The new place is really nice.
The monthly rent is a bit expensive.
grammar: 월세 (wolse) = monthly rent — 월 (month) + 세 (rent).

english: I also pay the maintenance fee every month.
Our home wifi is fast.
grammar: 빨라요 (ppallayo) = is fast, from 빠르다 (ppareuda).

english: The parking lot is underground.
grammar: 지하 (jiha) = underground — 지하철 is the 'underground train'!

english: The apartment playground is very big.
I clean the house every weekend.
grammar: 마다 (mada) = every: 주말마다 (jumalmada = every weekend).

english: I run the vacuum cleaner.
grammar: Koreans 'spin' machines: 청소기를 돌려요 (cheongsogireul dollyeoyo = run the vacuum).

english: In the afternoon I ran the washing machine too.
I did the laundry today.
grammar: 빨래 (ppallae) = laundry: 빨래를 해요 = do the laundry.

english: I do the dishes.
grammar: 설거지 (seolgeoji) = the dishes: 설거지를 해요 = wash the dishes.

english: I didn't do the dishes yesterday.
I tidied my room over the weekend.
I wiped the desk clean.
I wipe the floor with a rag.
I took out the trash.
grammar: 버려요 (beoryeoyo) = throw away: 쓰레기를 버려요 = take out the trash.

english: Cleaning the bathroom is really tough.
I washed the blankets.
grammar: 빨아요 (pparayo) = wash (fabric) — a special verb just for laundry!

english: I'll do the ironing in the afternoon.
I watered the flowers.
grammar: 물을 줘요 (mureul jwoyo) = 'give water' = to water plants.

english: There's so much housework.
grammar: 집안일 (jibanil) = housework — 'inside-the-house work.'

english: I felt good after cleaning.
Today we're doing a deep clean.
grammar: 대청소 (daecheongso) = the big all-day clean; 대- (dae) = big.

english: My younger sibling helped with the cleaning.
Mom cooks and Dad does the dishes.
I organized the fridge.
There's no milk in the fridge.
It was hot, so I turned on the AC.
grammar: 켜요 (kyeoyo) = turn on: 에어컨을 켜요 = turn on the AC.

english: I turn off the lights before bed.
grammar: -기 전에 (gi jeone) = before doing: 자기 전에 (jagi jeone = before sleeping).

english: I didn't turn off the room light.
grammar: 꺼요 (kkeoyo) = turn off, from 끄다 (kkeuda) — opposite of 켜요.

english: I closed the windows at night.
In Korea, people sort their recycling.
grammar: 분리수거 (bullisugeo) = mandatory trash sorting — an apartment-life ritual.

english: Bottles and cans go out separately.
grammar: 따로 (ttaro) = separately.

english: Plastic goes here.
I threw out the food waste separately.
grammar: 음식물 쓰레기 (eumsingmul sseuregi) = food waste — it gets its own bin in Korea.

english: Recycling day is every Thursday.
I threw out all the cardboard boxes.
I forgot the recycling yesterday.
grammar: 깜빡했어요 (kkamppakaesseoyo) = 'it slipped my mind' — the spoken way to say you forgot to do something.

english: I'll do the recycling this evening.
Tonight is delivery food again.
grammar: 배달 (baedal) = delivery — Korea's food-delivery culture is world-famous.

english: I ordered chicken on an app.
grammar: 시켜요 (sikyeoyo) = order (food): 치킨을 시켜요 = order chicken.

english: It arrives in thirty minutes.
The pizza is already here!
I ordered tteokbokki.
grammar: 떡볶이 (tteokbokki) = spicy rice cakes — Korea's favorite street food.

english: The delivery fee is 3,000 won.
grammar: -비 (bi) = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi) = delivery fee.

english: On weekends we often eat delivery food.
So I'm not cooking today.
The chicken hasn't come yet.
Please leave it at the door.
grammar: 문 앞에 놓아 주세요 (mun ape noa juseyo) — the delivery-app phrase.

english: The delivery came really fast.
What will you order for dinner?
I'll order bibimbap today.
Today I want to eat something with broth.
grammar: -고 싶어요 (go sipeoyo) = want to: 먹고 싶어요 = want to eat.

english: The weather is really nice today.
grammar: 날씨 (nalssi) = weather — Korea's small-talk opener.

english: It's raining outside.
grammar: 비가 와요 (biga wayo) = 'rain comes' — how Korean says it's raining.

english: Yesterday it rained all day long.
It will rain tomorrow too.
Do you have an umbrella?
The weather is too hot these days.
Last night it was a bit cold.
It's very windy today.
grammar: 바람이 불어요 (barami bureoyo) = the wind blows.

english: It's snowing outside!
grammar: 눈 (nun) = snow AND eye — context decides!

english: Last winter it snowed a lot.
The monsoon season has already started.
grammar: 장마 (jangma) = summer monsoon rains — guaranteed June small talk.

english: The fine dust is bad today.
grammar: 미세먼지 (misemeonji) = fine-dust pollution — Koreans check it like weather.

english: The sky is overcast.
In the afternoon the sky was clear.
The weather will be nice this weekend.
In spring lots of flowers bloom.
grammar: 봄 (bom) = spring; 펴요 (pyeoyo) = bloom.

english: I like autumn weather.
In winter the house is a bit cold.
On weekends I rest at home.
grammar: 쉬어요 (swieoyo) = rest, from 쉬다 (swida).

english: On Saturdays I sleep in late.
Yesterday I rested all day.
I took a nap on the sofa.
On Sundays I do nothing at all.
grammar: 아무것도 (amugeotdo) + negative = nothing at all.

english: This weekend I'm going to rest up.
grammar: 푹 쉬어요 (puk swieoyo) = rest deeply — wished to every tired friend.

english: I watched two movies at home.
