grammar: 편 (pyeon) counts movies and shows: 두 편 (du pyeon = two films).

english: I watched dramas all weekend.
I went to the Han River park with a friend.
grammar: 한강 (Hangang) = Seoul's river — picnics, bikes, and chicken.

english: Today I'm not going anywhere.
Did you rest well over the weekend?
grammar: Monday-morning Korean: 잘 쉬었어요? (jal swieosseoyo? = did you rest well?)

english: What are you doing next weekend?
I sent a text to my friend.
grammar: 문자 (munja) = text message: 문자를 보내요 = send a text.

english: Did you see my KakaoTalk message?
grammar: 카톡 (katok) = KakaoTalk — Korea's do-everything messaging app.

english: I sent the photos over KakaoTalk.
There's no reply yet.
I'll call a little later.
I called Mom yesterday.
I often video-call my grandmother.
grammar: 영상통화 (yeongsangtonghwa) = video call.

english: My phone battery is dead.
grammar: 배터리가 없어요 (baeteoriga eopseoyo) = 'no battery' = my phone's dying.

english: I left my phone at home.
grammar: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = left it behind — the forgot-it phrase.

english: What's the wifi password?
grammar: 비밀번호 (bimilbeonho) = password — literally 'secret number.'

english: I KakaoTalk with my family every day.
grammar: Add 하다 to anything: 카톡해요 (katokaeyo) = to message on KakaoTalk.

english: I changed my phone number.
I bought a new phone last week.
I took lots of photos at the Han River.
grammar: 사진을 찍어요 (sajineul jjigeoyo) = take a photo.

english: I took a selfie with my friend.
grammar: 셀카 (selka) = 'self-camera' = selfie — a Konglish classic.

english: The internet is slow today.
I use emoticons a lot.
grammar: 써요 (sseoyo) = use AND write — one verb, two jobs.

english: I don't look at my phone at night.
I set the alarm for six thirty.
I make the bed every morning.
grammar: 이불 (ibul) = blanket/bedding — you 'tidy' it, not 'make' it.

english: The cat sleeps on the sofa.
I take a walk with my dog every morning.
I made ramyeon in the evening.
grammar: 끓여요 (kkeuryeoyo) = boil up: 라면을 끓여요 = make ramyeon.

english: I baked bread at home over the weekend.
On Sunday mornings we have brunch.
I planted new flowers in the balcony pots.
grammar: 심어요 (simeoyo) = plant: 꽃을 심어요 = plant flowers.

english: There are family photos on the wall.
Our home is the best place in the world.
grammar: 제일 (jeil) = the most: 제일 좋아요 = like it best.

english: My head hurts so much.
grammar: 아프다 → 아파요 (apayo): body part + 이/가 아파요 = my X hurts.

english: My throat has been sore since yesterday.
I have a fever.
grammar: 열이 나요 (yeori nayo) = lit. a fever comes out — how Korean says "have a fever".

english: I am coughing a lot.
grammar: 기침을 해요 (gichimeul haeyo) = lit. "do a cough" — symptoms pair with 하다.

english: I have a runny nose too.
I caught a cold.
grammar: 감기에 걸렸어요 (gamgie geollyeosseoyo): catching a cold takes 에, not 을.

english: My stomach has hurt since last night.
I ache all over from a cold.
grammar: 몸살 (momsal) = the whole-body ache of a bad cold — it "breaks out": 났어요.

english: My throat is swollen.
grammar: 붓다 (butda) drops ㅅ before vowels: 부어요 (bueoyo) = it swells.

english: My nose is stuffed up.
I feel a little dizzy.
grammar: 어지럽다 → 어지러워요 (eojireowoyo): ㅂ turns into 워 before -어요.

english: My stomach feels off.
grammar: 속 (sok) = your insides: 속이 안 좋아요 = I feel queasy.

english: I have indigestion.
grammar: X이/가 안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) = X does not work: 소화가 안 돼요.

english: I have a bad toothache.
My back hurts so much that I cannot get up.
grammar: 못 (mot) before a verb = cannot: 못 일어나요 = can't get up.

english: My eyes are itchy.
I hurt my leg.
I hurt my ankle exercising yesterday.
My hand is a bit swollen.
My shoulders are stiff and achy.
grammar: 뻐근해요 (ppeogeunhaeyo) = stiff-achy — the desk-work neck-and-shoulder feeling.

english: My knee hurts, so stairs are hard.
grammar: -아/어서 (-aseo) = because: 아파서 = because it hurts.

target: 속이 안 좋아서 토할 것 같아요.
english: My stomach is upset — I feel like throwing up.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (geot gatayo) = feels like it will: 토할 것 같아요.

english: I am dizzy and I have a fever too.
grammar: -고 (-go) = and, linking verbs: 어지럽고 열도 나요.

english: I could not sleep at night because of the cough.
grammar: 때문에 (ttaemune) after a noun = because of: 기침 때문에.

english: My body has been constantly tired lately.
Your face is pale.

target: 오늘 몸이 안 좋아서 회사에 못 가요.
english: I am not feeling well today, so I cannot go to work.
I put in for sick leave with my department head.
grammar: Titled superiors take 께 (kke), not 한테: 부장님께 = to the manager.

english: I will get a good rest at home today.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) = a promise to the listener: 쉴게요 = I'll rest, I promise.

english: I will definitely come to work tomorrow.
A coworker caught a cold, so I am worried too.
The company president caught a cold too.
grammar: Honored subjects take -시-: 걸리셨어요 (geollisyeosseoyo), never 걸렸어요.

english: I will take my medicine before the meeting.
grammar: 약을 먹다 (yageul meokda) — Korean "eats" all medicine, even syrup.

english: I often get headaches because of stress.
I left work early because I felt unwell.
The office is dry, so my throat hurts.
I will pop out to the pharmacy at lunchtime.
grammar: 다녀오다 (danyeooda) = go and come back: 다녀올게요 = I'll be right back.

english: Don't push yourself — rest instead.
grammar: -지 말고 (-ji malgo) = don't do A, do B instead: 무리하지 말고 쉬세요.

english: I am going to the hospital this afternoon.
I made a hospital appointment for tomorrow.
Please register at the desk first.
grammar: 접수 (jeopsu) = check-in/registration at a desk: 접수를 해요.

english: Where does it hurt (what brings you in)?
grammar: Staff honor the customer: 오셨어요 (osyeosseoyo) = did you come + -시-.

english: Since when has it hurt?
It has hurt nonstop since last week.
How are your symptoms?
Do you also have a fever?
Let me take your temperature.
grammar: -아/어 볼게요 (bolgeyo) = I'll just try doing: 재 볼게요 = let me measure it.

english: Please sit here.
Take a deep breath.
grammar: 숨을 쉬다 (sumeul swida) = to breathe; 크게 (keuge) = big, deeply.

english: Your throat is quite swollen, I see.
It is a cold. Don't worry.
grammar: -지 마세요 (-ji maseyo) = please don't: 걱정하지 마세요 = don't worry.

english: You will get an injection today.
grammar: 주사를 맞다 (jusareul matda) = "receive" a shot — never 하다.

english: I got the shot. I am fine now.
I will prescribe you some medicine.
grammar: 드릴게요 (deurilgeyo) = I'll give — humble, done FOR the listener.

english: I received a prescription.
Take the prescription and go to the pharmacy.
How much is the consultation fee?
Do you have insurance?
Yes, I have travel insurance.
Did you bring your insurance card?
No, I left it at home.
grammar: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = left it behind — put it down and came.

english: The receipt too, please. I need it for the insurance.
Please come again next week.
I had a toothache, so I went to the dentist.
grammar: 치과 (chigwa) = dental clinic — -과 names the medical specialty.

english: My eyes kept itching, so I went to the eye doctor.
My child was sick, so we went to the pediatrician.
I waited an hour at the hospital.
Where is the pharmacy?
The pharmacy is right next to the hospital.
Is there a pharmacy around here?
Do you have cold medicine?
grammar: 감기약 (gamgiyak) = cold medicine — 감기 + 약 glued together.

english: Some cold medicine, please.
Do you have headache medicine too?
What symptoms do you have?
grammar: The pharmacist honors you: 있으세요 (isseuseyo) = honorific of 있어요.

english: I have a fever and a cough.
Take this medicine.
Take it three times a day.
grammar: 하루에 세 번 (harue se beon) = three times per day — 에 marks "per".

english: Take it after meals.
grammar: 식후 (sikhu) = after a meal; 식전 (sikjeon) = before a meal.

english: Is this medicine taken before meals?
Take one pill before you sleep.
grammar: -기 전에 (-gi jeone) = before doing: 자기 전에 = before sleeping.

english: This medicine is twice a day.
Take it together with water.
Take the medicine and sleep well.

target: 이 연고를 하루에 두 번 바르세요.
english: Apply this ointment twice a day.
grammar: 바르다 (bareuda) = spread on — creams, ointment, sunscreen.

english: I put ointment on the wound.
Some band-aids, please.
A pain-relief patch too, please.
grammar: 파스 (paseu) = stick-on pain patch — a Korean pharmacy staple.

english: Do you have something for indigestion?
grammar: 소화제 (sohwaje) = digestion aid; -제 = the medicine suffix.

english: Where are the fever reducers?
Do not drive after taking this medicine.
I am a bit drowsy after taking the medicine.
grammar: 졸려요 (jollyeoyo) = drowsy — different from 피곤해요 (tired).

english: I am allergic to this medicine.

target: 푹 쉬세요. 그리고 물을 많이 드세요.
english: Rest well. And drink plenty of water.
Don't overdo it.
grammar: 무리하다 (murihada) = push too hard: 무리하지 마세요 = take it easy.

english: You will be fine soon.
grammar: Adjective + -아/어지다 = become: 괜찮아지다 (gwaenchanajida) = get better.

english: My cold is completely better.
grammar: 낫다 (natda) = to heal; ㅅ drops: 나았어요 (naasseoyo) = it got better.

english: My throat does not hurt anymore.
I am much better than yesterday.
grammar: 보다 (boda) after a noun = than: 어제보다 = than yesterday.

english: The fever went down.
I do not cough anymore.
Take good care of yourself.
grammar: 몸조리 잘하세요 (momjori jalhaseyo) — the set phrase for "get well soon".

english: My grandmother has been unwell lately.
grammar: Elders don't 아프다 — they 편찮으시다: 편찮으세요 (pyeonchanuseyo).

english: My grandfather's knees hurt.
grammar: An elder's pain still takes -시-: 아프세요 (apeuseyo), not 아파요.

english: My mother caught a cold.
My father got a health checkup last week.
My parents are both healthy.
grammar: 분 (bun) = honorific counter for people: 두 분 = two (respected) people.

english: My younger sibling hurt their leg and went to the hospital.
My child has a fever, so I am worried.
The baby coughed all night long.
I made rice porridge for my grandmother.
grammar: -어 드려요 (deuryeoyo) = do for an elder — humble version of -어 줘요.

english: The whole family caught colds.
Colds are going around among the kids.
grammar: 유행 (yuhaeng) = going around — fashion AND flu can both 유행이에요.

english: Wash your hands often.
For preventing colds, hand-washing is key.
grammar: -기 (-gi) makes a verb into a noun: 씻기 (ssitgi) = washing.

english: I take vitamins every day.
Exercise is good for your health.
grammar: X에 좋아요 (e joayo) = good for X: 건강에 좋아요.

english: Cigarettes are bad for your body.
I have not been sleeping well lately.
I got an upset stomach while traveling.
grammar: 배탈이 나다 (baetari nada) = get a stomach bug — it "breaks out".

english: Do you have motion-sickness medicine?
grammar: 멀미 (meolmi) = motion sickness; 멀미약 = the pill for it.

english: I got carsick on the bus.
Do you sell painkillers here?
My Korean is not good, so please help me.
Please go with me to the hospital.
grammar: -아/어 주세요 (juseyo) = do it for me: 가 주세요 = please go (with me).

english: Prepare basic medicines before your trip.
grammar: 상비약 (sangbiyak) = always-ready medicines — the home first-aid stash.

english: The weather is really nice today, isn't it!
grammar: -네요 (-neyo) = shared surprise: 좋네요 = it's nice, isn't it!

english: Yes, the sky is really clear.
The sky is a bit overcast today.
It is very cloudy.
It is very windy.
Yesterday the wind blew hard.
There was fog in the morning.
grammar: 안개가 끼다 (angaega kkida) = fog "settles in": 안개가 꼈어요.

english: The weather suddenly turned cold.
It is still warm during the day.
It is chilly in the mornings and evenings.
grammar: 쌀쌀해요 (ssalssalhaeyo) = crisp-chilly — jacket weather, not coat weather.

english: The day-night temperature gap is big these days.
grammar: 일교차 (ilgyocha) = day-night temperature gap — a weather-talk favorite.

english: It is easy to catch a cold between seasons.
grammar: -기 쉬워요 (-gi swiwoyo) = easy to do: 걸리기 쉬워요.

english: Watch out for colds.
Is it very cold outside?
Yes, wear a coat.
What are you going to wear today?
In winter the air is very dry.
How is the weather today?
What will next week's weather be like?
Did you check the weather forecast?
It looks like rain this afternoon.
Be sure to take an umbrella.
It rained in the morning. It has stopped now.
grammar: 그치다 (geuchida) = (rain or snow) stops: 비가 그쳤어요.

english: It is drizzling.
grammar: -씩 (-ssik) = bit by bit: 조금씩 = little by little.

english: A sudden shower came down.
grammar: 소나기 (sonagi) = a short, sudden rain shower.

english: I got caught in the rain and my clothes got soaked.
grammar: 비를 맞다 (bireul matda) = get rained on — you "receive" the rain.

english: I left my umbrella on the bus.
I bought an umbrella at a convenience store.
I put on rain boots and went out.
There was thunder.
grammar: 천둥이 치다 (cheondungi chida) — thunder "strikes" in Korean.

english: There was lightning too.
A typhoon is coming.
grammar: -고 있어요 (-go isseoyo) = is ...ing right now: 오고 있어요 = is coming.

english: A typhoon is coming tomorrow. Please be careful.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (-l geoyeyo) = will / is going to: 올 거예요 = it will come.

english: The window rattled because of the wind.
We canceled soccer because of the rain.
It rained, so we watched a movie at home.
The plane was delayed because of the weather.
The first snow fell!
grammar: 첫눈 (cheonnun) = the year's first snow — practically a holiday in Korea.

english: It is snowing thick and fast outside.
grammar: 펑펑 (peongpeong) — the sound of fat snowflakes falling thick.

english: The road is icy and slippery.
I fell down on the snowy road.
It is minus five degrees today.
grammar: 영하 (yeongha) = below zero: 영하 5도 = minus 5 degrees.

english: The temperature dropped a lot last night.
How many degrees is it today?
grammar: 몇 도예요? (myeot doyeyo) — degrees ride on Sino numbers: 오 도, 이십 도.

english: It is 25 degrees right now.
The temperature will drop to 3 degrees in the morning.
The temperature climbs a lot during the day.
Today is colder than yesterday.
I put on gloves.
grammar: 끼다 (kkida) = wear things that slide on — gloves, rings, glasses.

english: I put on a scarf and went out.
grammar: 목도리를 하다 (mokdorireul hada) — scarves are "done", not worn.

english: It is too cold without a padded coat.
grammar: 패딩 (paeding) = the long puffer coat — Korea's winter uniform.

english: My hands froze stiff.
The kids built a snowman.
We had a snowball fight in the park.
It was cold, so I turned on the boiler.
grammar: 보일러 (boilleo) heats the floor (온돌, ondol) — warmth from below.

english: In winter I often buy bungeoppang to eat.
grammar: 붕어빵 (bungeoppang) = fish-shaped winter street bread, sweet red bean inside.

english: We went to a ski resort during winter break.
The snow has melted.
The cold has finally eased up.
grammar: 날씨가 풀리다 (pullida) — the cold "loosens" when a freeze ends.

english: Spring is here. Flowers have started to bloom.
grammar: -기 시작하다 = start to do: 피기 시작했어요 = started blooming.

english: The cherry blossoms are so pretty in spring.
grammar: 벚꽃 (beotkkot) season lasts barely a week — Koreans track the bloom forecast.

english: We went cherry-blossom viewing on the weekend.
I took lots of blossom photos at the Han River.
The cherry blossoms have already all fallen.
I see the cherry blossoms with my family every year.
The spring breeze is really warm.
The weather is just right for a picnic.
In spring the yellow dust gets bad.
grammar: 황사 (hwangsa) = spring's yellow desert dust that blows into Korea.

english: The fine dust is bad today.
grammar: 미세먼지 (misemeonji) = fine dust — Koreans check its index like weather.

english: Wear a mask when you go outside.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ 때 (ttae) = when doing: 나갈 때 = when going out.

english: The air was bad, so I closed the windows.
I have a pollen allergy.
I put away winter clothes and got out spring clothes.
In April it is sometimes cold.
The weather was nice, so I took a walk in the park.
Korean summers are really hot.
It is hot and humid.
grammar: 습해요 (seuphaeyo) = humid — summer's real hardship in Korea.

english: In monsoon season it rains almost every day.
grammar: 장마 (jangma) = the summer rainy weeks — late June into July.

english: The monsoon will start soon.
The rainy season will end next week.
In monsoon season the laundry does not dry well.
grammar: 마르다 → 말라요 (mallayo): 르-verbs double the ㄹ.

english: It was so hot that I turned on the air conditioner.
The air-conditioner draft is too strong.
It is hot even at night, so I cannot fall asleep.
grammar: 잠이 안 와요 (jami an wayo) — sleep "won't come" = can't fall asleep.

english: Last night was a tropical night.
grammar: 열대야 (yeoldaeya) = a night that stays above 25 degrees — sleepless summer.

english: In summer we eat patbingsu.
grammar: 팥빙수 (patbingsu) = shaved-ice mountain with sweet red beans on top.

english: On the dog days we eat samgyetang.
grammar: 복날 (boknal) = hottest days — Koreans beat heat with hot ginseng-chicken soup.

english: I am sweating a lot.
The UV is strong. Put on sunscreen.
When it is hot, drink lots of water.
I want to go to the ocean in summer.
grammar: -고 싶어요 (-go sipeoyo) = want to: 가고 싶어요 = I want to go.

english: On vacation we went to a valley stream with my family.
We canceled our trip because of the typhoon.
The autumn sky is really high.
grammar: Koreans praise fall skies as "high": 하늘이 높아요 (haneuri nopayo).

english: In October the leaves turn.
grammar: 단풍이 들다 (danpungi deulda) = leaves "take on" their fall colors.

english: We went to Mt. Seorak to see the fall leaves.
The autumn leaves were really beautiful.
A lot of dead leaves have fallen.
Autumn is the season of reading.
grammar: Koreans call fall 독서의 계절 (dokseoui gyejeol) — the reading season.

english: In autumn the weather is pleasantly cool.
grammar: 선선해요 (seonseonhaeyo) = pleasantly cool — autumn's own word.

english: The weather was nice at Chuseok.
Which season do you like best?
I like autumn the best.
I like summer better than winter.
Korea has four distinct seasons.
grammar: 사계절 (sagyejeol) = the four seasons — a point of Korean pride.

english: Of the four seasons, spring is the shortest.
grammar: N 중에서 (jungeseo) = among N: 사계절 중에서 = among the four seasons.

english: Is it snowing in Seoul right now?
Busan is warmer than Seoul.
Jeju Island is famous for its wind.
grammar: 제주 is 삼다도 (samdado) — the island of three manys: wind, stones, women.

english: It is cloudy and cold.
The sky is gray today.
A rainbow came out!
grammar: 뜨다 (tteuda) = rise, come up: sun, moon, rainbows all 떠요 (tteoyo).

english: The sun came back out.
The roads were badly jammed because of the snow.

target: 내일 눈이 올 거예요. 그래서 일찍 출발할 거예요.
english: It will snow tomorrow. So we will leave early.
The weather will probably be nice this weekend.
When the weather is good, I go hiking.
In winter the sun sets early.
grammar: 해가 지다 (haega jida) = the sun sets; 해가 뜨다 = it rises.

english: In summer the sun sets late.
Tonight you can see a lot of stars.
I am waiting for spring.
My grandmother really feels the cold.
grammar: 할머니 is honored: 타세요 (taseyo) — the -시- respect marker on 타다.

english: I suffer badly in the heat.
grammar: 더위/추위를 타다 (tada) = "ride" the heat/cold = be sensitive to it.

english: Kids really love snow.

target: 내년 봄에 한국에 갈 거예요. 벚꽃을 보고 싶어요.
english: Next spring I will go to Korea. I want to see the cherry blossoms.
What's your hobby?
grammar: 취미 (chwimi) = hobby — Korea's standard get-to-know-you question.

english: My hobby is hiking.
grammar: Answer with noun + 이에요: 제 취미는 등산이에요 (deungsan-ieyo) = my hobby is hiking.

english: I go hiking every weekend.
grammar: 마다 (mada) = every: 주말마다 (jumalmada) = every weekend.

english: What sports do you like?
I don't really like exercise.
What do you usually do on weekends?
I started a new hobby.
We have the same hobby.
I like quiet hobbies.
grammar: Descriptive verbs take -ㄴ before nouns: 조용한 취미 (joyonghan chwimi) = a quiet hobby.

english: It's good to have a hobby.
grammar: -(으)면 = if: 취미가 있으면 (isseumyeon) = if you have a hobby.

english: My little sibling has so many hobbies.
I want to learn the guitar.
Koreans really love hiking.
grammar: 등산 (deungsan) = hiking — Korea's national hobby; most of the country is mountains.

english: I'm going to Bukhansan tomorrow morning.
I bought new hiking boots.
We ate gimbap at the summit.
grammar: 정상 (jeongsang) = summit — where Korean hikers unpack their gimbap.

english: It took two hours to the top.
Shall we go hiking together next weekend?
grammar: -(으)ㄹ까요? = shall we?: 같이 등산할까요? (gachi deungsanhalkkayo?)

english: The mountain air is so refreshing.
We drank makgeolli after the hike.
grammar: 후에 (hue) = after: 등산 후에 = after hiking — makgeolli is the classic reward.

english: The mountain was so crowded on the weekend.
Dad goes to the mountains every Sunday.
grammar: -세요 respects the subject: 아빠는 가세요 (gaseyo); for yourself, 가요.

english: I don't like high mountains.
grammar: 높다 → 높은 before a noun: 높은 산 (nopeun san) = a high mountain.

english: At first, a low mountain is best.
I put water and snacks in my hiking bag.
We got lost on the mountain.
In autumn the leaves are really beautiful.
grammar: 단풍 (danpung) = autumn foliage — peak hiking season in Korea.

english: I go to the gym every morning.
grammar: 헬스장 (helseujang) = gym — Konglish, from English 'health'.

english: When did you join the gym?
grammar: 등록하다 (deungnokada) = to register, sign up: 헬스장에 등록했어요.

english: I worked out too much yesterday.
My arms and legs hurt today.
I do yoga twice a week.
grammar: 번 (beon) counts times, with native numbers: 두 번 (du beon) = twice.

english: I drink lots of water after working out.
My weight has gone down a little recently.
grammar: 줄다 (julda) = to decrease: 몸무게가 줄었어요 (mommugega jureosseoyo) = my weight went down.

english: I want to start exercising again.
I work out at the gym after work.
I was too tired today, so I rested.
grammar: -아/어서 = so, because: 피곤해서 쉬었어요 (pigonhaeseo) = tired, so I rested.

english: From tomorrow I'll run in the mornings.
I rode a bike by the Han River yesterday.
I want to buy a new bicycle.
I want to learn to swim.
Shall we go to the pool together?
I play soccer every Saturday.
grammar: 매주 (maeju) = every week: 매주 토요일 = every Saturday.

english: Our team won yesterday.
grammar: 이기다 (igida) = to win: 팀이 이겼어요 = the team won.

english: We lost today's game.
grammar: 지다 (jida) = to lose: 경기에서 졌어요 = lost the game.

english: I went to watch a baseball game.
grammar: -(으)러 가다 = go to (do): 보러 갔어요 (boreo gasseoyo) = went to watch.

english: I like baseball more than soccer.
grammar: N보다 (boda) = than: 축구보다 = (more) than soccer.

english: Which team do you root for?
Do you play tennis often?
grammar: 치다 (chida) = hit — for tennis, badminton, piano, guitar: 테니스를 쳐요.

english: I played badminton with a friend on the weekend.
I'm going skiing in the winter.
I watch the game at home in the evening.
I saw a movie at the theater with my family.
I saw three movies last month.
grammar: 편 (pyeon) counts films: 세 편 (se pyeon) = three (movies).

english: What kind of movies do you like best?
I like comedies.
grammar: 좋아해요 takes 을/를 (I like it); 좋아요 takes 이/가 (it's good): 영화를 좋아해요 / 영화가 좋아요.

english: This movie is really fun.
I booked the tickets in advance.
grammar: 미리 (miri) = in advance: 미리 예매했어요 = booked ahead.

english: I can't watch a movie without popcorn.
grammar: 없이 (eopsi) = without: 팝콘 없이 = without popcorn.

english: What drama are you watching these days?
That drama is so sad.
I watched a drama until dawn yesterday.
grammar: 새벽 (saebyeok) = dawn, the small hours: 새벽까지 = until dawn.

english: I can't wait for the next episode.
grammar: 궁금하다 (gunggeumhada) = be curious: 다음 회가 궁금해요 = dying to know what's next.

target: 드라마 한 시즌을 하루 만에 다 봤어요.
english: I binged a whole season in one day.
grammar: 만에 (mane) = in (just): 하루 만에 = in a single day.

english: Do you like Korean movies?
I really like that actor.
The movie ended at 10 p.m.
I'm reading an interesting book these days.
grammar: 있다·없다 adjectives take -는: 재미있는 책 (jaemiinneun chaek) = an interesting book; other adjectives take -(으)ㄴ (예쁜).

target: 한 달에 책을 두 권 읽어요.
english: I read two books a month.
grammar: 권 (gwon) counts books: 두 권 (du gwon) = two books.

english: I borrowed a book from the library.
grammar: 빌리다 (billida) = to borrow: 책을 빌렸어요 = borrowed a book.

english: I read at a cafe on the weekend.
This novel was really good.
I read a little before bed.
grammar: V-기 전에 = before V-ing: 자기 전에 (jagi jeone) = before sleeping.

english: What book do you recommend?
That author's new book is out.
I sometimes read comics too.
I read books and talk about them with a friend.
I really love games.

target: 어제 밤에 게임을 세 시간 했어요.
english: I played games for three hours last night.
grammar: 시간 (sigan) counts hours, native numbers: 세 시간 = three hours.

english: I played games with my little brother.
This game is really hard.
My friend is really good at games.
grammar: 잘하다 (jalhada) = be good at: 게임을 잘해요 = good at games.

english: I lost the game again.
This time I won.
grammar: 제가 (jega) = 저 + subject marker 가: 제가 이겼어요 = I won.

english: I played phone games way too long.
Our son does nothing but game.
grammar: 만 (man) = only: 게임만 해요 = only plays games.

english: Exercise is better for you than games.
We went to karaoke on Friday night.
grammar: 노래방 (noraebang) = karaoke room — the classic end to a night out in Korea.

english: We sang for two hours at karaoke.
grammar: 동안 (dongan) = for, during: 두 시간 동안 = for two hours.

english: What song do you sing best?
grammar: 부르다 → 불러요 (bulleoyo): 노래를 불러요 = sing a song.

english: My friend sings really well.
I can't sing well.
grammar: 잘 못 (jal mot) = can't do well: 잘 못 불러요 = can't sing well.

english: I blow off stress at karaoke.
grammar: 스트레스를 풀다 (pulda) = relieve stress, lit. 'untie' it: 스트레스를 풀어요.

english: I want to learn Korean songs.
Shall we hit karaoke again?
Taking photos is my hobby.
grammar: V-기 turns a verb into a noun: 사진 찍기 (sajin jjikgi) = taking photos.

english: I took photos in the park on the weekend.
I want to buy a new camera.
I took lots of flower photos.
This photo came out great.
I took a hundred photos on the trip.
grammar: 장 (jang) counts flat things — photos, tickets, paper: 백 장 = 100 shots.

english: I often photograph the sky.
The sunset was gorgeous today.
I shoot with my phone more than my camera.
grammar: 더 (deo) = more: 카메라보다 더 자주 = more often than the camera; (으)로 marks the tool (핸드폰으로).

english: I take a photography class.
grammar: -(으)러 + 가다/다니다 = go (to do): 배우러 다녀요 (baeureo danyeoyo) = attend to learn.

english: What did you do last weekend?
I slept in on Saturday.
On Sunday I rested up at home.
grammar: 푹 (puk) = deeply (rest, sleep): 푹 쉬었어요 = got a good rest.

english: Did you have a good weekend?
grammar: 주말 잘 보냈어요? (jumal jal bonaesseoyo?) — the standard Monday greeting.

english: Yes, it was great.
I did absolutely nothing this weekend.
grammar: 아무것도 + 안 = nothing: 아무것도 안 했어요 (amugeotdo an haesseoyo).

english: I went to a friend's wedding.
We ate out as a family.
I got all the housework done.
I did laundry and cleaned over the weekend.
What are you doing this weekend?
I'm meeting a friend on Saturday.
Sunday I'll just stay home.
grammar: 그냥 (geunyang) = just: 그냥 집에 있을 거예요 = just staying in.

english: If the weather's nice, I'll go hiking.
grammar: -(으)면 = if: 날씨가 좋으면 (joeumyeon) = if the weather is good.

english: We're going camping next weekend.
We grilled meat at the campsite.
We went to the sea to fish.
I have no plans at all.
The weekend is too short.
It's already Monday.
Did you get a new phone?
My phone is really old.
grammar: 오래되다 (oraedoeda) = be old (things): 오래됐어요 = it's gotten old.

english: I'm on my phone all day.
grammar: 하루 종일 (haru jongil) = all day long.

english: What's your KakaoTalk ID?
grammar: 카톡 (katok) = KakaoTalk — Korea's default messenger; 'text me' is 카톡해요.

english: Message me on KakaoTalk.
grammar: 연락하다 (yeollakada) = to contact: 카톡으로 연락해요 = reach me by KakaoTalk.

english: I'll message you later.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ게요 = I'll (a promise to the listener): 카톡할게요 (katokhalgeyo).

english: I posted the photo in the group chat.
grammar: 단톡방 (dantokbang) = group chat — group + KakaoTalk + room.

english: I haven't read the message yet.
The reply came so late.
I use stickers a lot.
grammar: 쓰다 (sseuda) = use (also 'write'): 이모티콘을 써요 = I use (KakaoTalk) stickers.

english: I replied to Mom.
I message my friend every day.
Could you give me your phone number?
grammar: 좀 (jom) softens requests: 좀 알려 주세요 (jom allyeo juseyo) = please let me know.

english: The new phone is really light.
The screen is really big.
I changed my ringtone.

target: 회의 중에는 휴대폰을 무음으로 해 놓아요.
english: I keep my phone on silent in meetings.
grammar: 무음으로 해 놓아요 (hae noayo) — -아/어 놓다 marks a kept state: leave it on silent; N 중에 = during.

english: Everyone on the subway is glued to their phone.
Is there wifi here?
The wifi suddenly cut out.
grammar: 끊기다 (kkeunkida) = get cut off: 와이파이가 끊겼어요 = the wifi dropped.

english: The cafe wifi is free.
grammar: 무료 (muryo) = free of charge: 무료예요 = it's free.

english: I typed the password in again.
grammar: 입력하다 (imnyeokada) = to enter, type in: 비밀번호를 입력해요.

english: Why is the internet this slow?
I used up all my data.
grammar: 다 쓰다 = use up: 데이터를 다 썼어요 (da sseosseoyo) = data's all gone.

english: The hotel internet was a bit slow.
The internet barely works here.
I bought a SIM at the airport.
grammar: 유심 (yusim) = SIM card — a traveler's first purchase at the airport.

english: I'm almost out of data.
I forgot the wifi password again.
I read the news online.
The battery's dead.
grammar: 배터리가 다 됐어요 (da dwaesseoyo) = battery's done — the everyday 'it died'.

english: My battery's almost gone.
Could you lend me a charger?
grammar: V-어 주세요 = please (do for me): 빌려 주세요 (billyeo juseyo) = please lend me.

english: I left my charger at home.
My phone is charging.
grammar: -고 있어요 = is ...ing: 충전하고 있어요 (chungjeonhago isseoyo) = is charging.

english: I always carry a power bank.
grammar: 보조 배터리 (bojo baeteori) = power bank — 'auxiliary battery'.

english: Where can I charge?
grammar: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 = can: 충전할 수 있어요? (chungjeonhal su isseoyo?) = can I charge?

english: Does the cafe have outlets?
I charge my phone at night.
The battery drains fast.
grammar: 닳다 (talta) = wear down: 배터리가 닳아요 = the battery drains.

english: The charging cable broke again.
grammar: 고장 나다 (gojang nada) = break down: 고장 났어요 = it broke.

english: The new charger is really fast.
Give this app a try.
grammar: V-어 보세요 = try ...ing: 써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try it out.

english: I installed a new app.
grammar: 설치하다 (seolchihada) = to install: 앱을 설치했어요.

english: Is this app free?

target: 지도 앱 없이 여행을 못 해요.
english: I can't travel without a map app.
I check bus times on an app.
I updated the app.
I deleted several apps.
grammar: 삭제하다 (sakjehada) = to delete: 앱을 삭제했어요 = deleted apps.

english: I sent money with my banking app.
I ordered dinner on a delivery app.
I set my alarm for seven.
grammar: 알람을 맞추다 (matchuda) = set an alarm: 일곱 시에 맞췄어요.

english: This app is so convenient.
The kids watch too much YouTube.
I learned to cook from YouTube.
I listen to music on an app.
I couldn't log into the app.
grammar: 못 (mot) = can't: 로그인을 못 했어요 = couldn't log in.

english: Shall we take a selfie here?
We took a group photo with friends.
I posted the photo on Instagram.
grammar: 올리다 (ollida) = upload, post: 사진을 올렸어요 = posted a photo.

english: I changed my profile picture.
This filter is so pretty.
I backed the photos up to the cloud.
grammar: 저장하다 (jeojanghada) = to save: 클라우드에 저장했어요.

english: I deleted all my old photos.
grammar: 지우다 (jiuda) = to erase, delete: 사진을 지웠어요.

english: I'm editing a video.
grammar: 편집하다 (pyeonjipada) = to edit: 영상을 편집해요.

english: The video is too long.
I got a lot of comments.
grammar: 댓글 (daetgeul) = comment (online): 댓글을 받았어요.

english: My phone broke.
The screen cracked.
grammar: 깨지다 (kkaejida) = crack, shatter: 화면이 깨졌어요 = the screen cracked.

english: I dropped my phone on the floor.
grammar: 떨어뜨리다 (tteoreotteurida) = to drop: 휴대폰을 떨어뜨렸어요.

english: My phone suddenly shut off.
grammar: 꺼지다 (kkeojida) = go off (by itself): 갑자기 꺼졌어요.

english: My phone is burning hot.
There's no sound.
grammar: 소리가 나다 (soriga nada) = make sound: 소리가 안 나요 = no sound comes out.

english: I went to the service center.
The repair fee was way too much.
grammar: 수리비 (suribi) = repair cost — 비 (bi) = fee: 택시비, 수리비.

english: I got the screen replaced.
I dropped my phone in water.
grammar: 빠뜨리다 (ppatteurida) = drop into: 물에 빠뜨렸어요 = dropped it in water.

english: Thankfully it works fine now.
I turned the phone back on.
Press and hold the power button.
grammar: -게 makes adverbs: 길게 (gilge) = long → 길게 눌러요 = long-press.

english: Just tap here.
grammar: -(으)면 돼요 = just do X: 누르면 돼요 (nureumyeon dwaeyo) = pressing works.

english: My phone froze again.
I bought clothes online.
I shop online way too often.
grammar: 온라인 (ollain) = online: 온라인 쇼핑 = online shopping.

english: This site is the cheapest.
The clothes I ordered haven't arrived.
grammar: V-ㄴ + noun = that I ...ed: 주문한 옷 (jumunhan ot) = the clothes I ordered.

english: The package finally came.
grammar: 드디어 (deudieo) = finally: 드디어 왔어요 = it finally arrived.

english: Shipping was super fast.
grammar: 배송 (baesong) = delivery, shipping: 배송이 빨라요 = shipping is fast.

english: It arrives tomorrow morning.
It didn't fit, so I got a refund.
grammar: -아서 = so: 안 맞아서 환불했어요 (an majaseo hwanbulhaesseoyo).

english: I read the reviews first.
The rating is really high.
grammar: 별점 (byeoljeom) = star rating: 별점이 높아요 = highly rated.

english: I paid by card.
grammar: 결제하다 (gyeoljehada) = to pay, check out: 카드로 결제했어요.

english: I want to cancel my order.
grammar: 취소하다 (chwisohada) = to cancel: 주문을 취소해요.

english: I bought shoes during the sale.
grammar: N 때 (ttae) = at the time of: 세일 때 = during the sale.

english: I saved 10,000 won with a coupon.
grammar: 아끼다 (akkida) = to save (money): 만 원을 아꼈어요.

english: My cart is full of clothes.
Can you talk right now?
grammar: 통화하다 (tonghwahada) = talk on the phone: 통화할 수 있어요? = free to talk?

english: I'm a bit busy right now.
I'll call you back in a bit.
I missed your call.
I texted you twice.
I left a voicemail.
grammar: 남기다 (namgida) = to leave (behind): 메시지를 남겼어요 = left a message.

english: I dialed the wrong number.
grammar: 잘못 (jalmot) = wrongly: 잘못 눌렀어요 = pressed wrong.

english: I don't pick up unknown numbers.
Grandma loves video calls.
grammar: Honored subjects take -세요: 할머니는 좋아하세요 (joahaseyo).

english: I video-called Dad.
I bought a new laptop.
grammar: 노트북 (noteubuk) = laptop (Konglish) — a paper notebook is 공책.

english: My computer is so slow.
Did you save the file?
Please send it by email.
The printer broke again.
I left my earphones on the subway.
Wireless earphones are so convenient.
grammar: 무선 (museon) = wireless, lit. 'no wire': 무선 이어폰 = wireless earbuds.

english: I turned the computer off and on again.
I change my password often.
My work computer won't turn on today.
grammar: 켜지다 (kyeojida) = turn on (by itself): 안 켜져요 = won't turn on.

english: Please turn your phone off in the theater.
Don't look at your phone while driving.
grammar: -지 마세요 = please don't: 보지 마세요 (boji maseyo) = don't look.

target: 자기 전에 휴대폰을 너무 오래 봐요.
english: I'm on my phone too long before bed.
I put my phone down when I eat.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ 때 = when: 먹을 때 (meogeul ttae) = when eating.

english: How many hours a day are you on your phone?
On weekends I keep phone time short.
I checked my screen time and was shocked.
grammar: 깜짝 놀라다 (kkamjjak nollada) = be startled: 깜짝 놀랐어요.

english: I can't live without the internet.
grammar: 없이 못 살아요 (eopsi mot sarayo) = can't live without it.

english: Seollal is the lunar New Year.
grammar: 음력 (eumnyeok) = lunar calendar; 설날 follows it, not January 1.

english: On Seollal the whole family gathers.
grammar: 온 (on) before a noun = the whole: 온 가족 = the whole family.

target: 설날 아침에 다 같이 떡국을 먹어요.
english: On Seollal morning we all eat tteokguk together.

target: 떡국을 먹으면 한 살 더 먹어요.
english: When you eat tteokguk, you turn a year older.
grammar: 나이를 먹다 (nai-reul meokda) = to "eat" age; 한 살 더 먹어요 = a year older.

target: 그래서 설날에 나이를 한 살 먹어요.
english: So on Seollal everyone gains a year of age.
On Seollal morning we wear hanbok.
The hanbok with pretty colors is really lovely.
The children give the elders a deep New Year bow.
grammar: 께 (kke) = honorific "to"; 어른들께 = to the elders.

english: The New Year bow is offered respectfully as a full bow.
grammar: 드리다 (deurida) is the humble "give": 세배를 드려요 = I bow to my elders.

english: After bowing, the children receive New Year money.
grammar: 세뱃돈 (setbaetdon) = New Year money, given after 세배, not before.

english: Grandmother gave me New Year money.
grammar: 께서 (kkeseo) marks an honored subject; the verb takes 주셨어요 (jusyeosseoyo).

english: New Year money is usually given in fresh bills.
The New Year money is put in an envelope to give.
The kids are really happy to get their New Year money.
grammar: 3rd-person feelings take -어하다: 아이들이 기뻐해요 (gippeohaeyo = they're happy).

english: The elders offer the children words of blessing.
grammar: 덕담 (deokdam) = kind New Year words an elder gives a younger person.

english: Grandfather gave us a warm word of blessing.
On Seollal we hold the ancestral rite for our forebears.
grammar: 차례 (charye) = the holiday ancestral rite; 지내다 = to hold it.

english: We set the rite table with food, with great care.
The whole family bows to the ancestors.
All the relatives gather at the head family's house.
grammar: 큰집 (keunjip) = the eldest son's household, where the rite is held.

english: The Seollal holiday usually lasts three days.
grammar: 사흘 (saheul) = three days (native count), used for spans of time.

english: During the holidays the road home gets very congested.

target: 고향 가는 기차표가 벌써 다 팔렸어요.
english: The train tickets home are already all sold out.
grammar: 팔리다 → 팔렸어요 (pallyeosseoyo) = got sold; the passive of 팔다.

english: The trip home took a full five hours.
grammar: -이나 (-ina) after a number stresses it's a lot: 다섯 시간이나 = as much as five hours.

english: We rested for a bit at the highway rest stop.
On Seollal the whole family plays yut.
grammar: 윷놀이 (yunnori) = a stick-tossing board game families play at Seollal.

english: Playing yut, everyone laughs together.
The children fly kites and play.

target: 설날 아침에 떡국 한 그릇을 비웠어요.
english: I finished a whole bowl of tteokguk on Seollal morning.
Grandmother also made dumplings by hand.
At Seollal I meet relatives I haven't seen in a while.
grammar: 오랜만에 (oraenmane) = after a long time, for the first time in ages.

english: I talked with my cousins late into the night.
May you receive many blessings this new year.
grammar: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo) = the set New Year greeting.

english: We give the elders our New Year greetings.
After Seollal passes, school starts again.
Chuseok is a big holiday that comes in autumn.
grammar: 추석 (Chuseok) = the autumn harvest holiday, Korea's Thanksgiving.

english: At Chuseok we make songpyeon.
grammar: 송편 (songpyeon) = half-moon rice cakes shaped by hand for Chuseok.

english: The whole family sits around and shapes songpyeon.

target: 송편을 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 아기를 낳는대요.
english: They say if you shape songpyeon prettily, you'll have a pretty baby.
grammar: -대요 (-daeyo) reports a saying: 낳는대요 = they say one will have (a baby).

english: We put sesame and beans inside the songpyeon.
At Chuseok as well we hold the ancestral rite.
We set the table carefully with the year's new grain.
grammar: 햇- (haet-) before a food means "this year's first": 햇곡식 = new-harvest grain.

english: On Chuseok morning we visit the ancestral graves.
grammar: 성묘 (seongmyo) = visiting and tending the family graves.

english: We go to the grave site and bow.
Before the grave visit we clear the grass in advance.
grammar: 벌초 (beolcho) = cutting the grass around ancestral graves before Chuseok.

english: We cut the grass at Grandfather's grave.
On Chuseok evening we look at the full moon.
grammar: 보름달 (boreumdal) = the full moon; Chuseok falls on a full-moon night.

english: Looking at the full moon, we make a wish.
grammar: 소원을 빌다 (sowon-eul bilda) = to make a wish.

english: It's a good harvest year again, so we feel content.
During the Chuseok holiday the roads home are really jammed.
The road to my hometown was terribly congested.
grammar: 고향 (gohyang) = one's hometown, where the family gathers.

english: Even so, I'm happy to see my family.
At Chuseok the relatives gather at the head family's house.
I met my younger cousin for the first time in ages.
Mother is frying savory pancakes.
grammar: 전을 부치다 (jeon-eul buchida) = to pan-fry Korean holiday pancakes.

english: The kitchen is full of the smell of frying oil.
We make japchae and galbi together as well.

target: 추석 음식을 다 같이 나눠 먹어요.
english: We all share the Chuseok food together.
After the rite we divide up the food.
At Chuseok we dress up nicely in hanbok.
The full moon is really bright and round.

target: 가족과 함께 있어서 이번 추석이 더 좋아요.
english: This Chuseok is better because I'm with family.
Parents' Day is May 8th.
grammar: 어버이날 (eobeoinal) = Parents' Day; 오월 팔일 (Sino numbers) = May 8.

english: On Parents' Day we give our parents carnations.
grammar: 카네이션 (kaneisyeon) = the carnation given to parents on this day.

english: We pin a carnation on our parents' chest.
grammar: 달아 드리다 (dara deurida) = to pin (it) on for someone, humbly.

english: The red carnation is really pretty.
We express our gratitude to our parents.
grammar: 감사한 마음 (gamsahan maeum) = a grateful heart; 전하다 = to convey it.

english: On Parents' Day I wrote a letter and gave it to them.
I took my parents out and we had dinner.
grammar: 모시다 (mosida) = to accompany an elder respectfully; 모시고 = escorting them.

english: Thank you for giving me life and raising me.
My parents always cherish me.
It's a small gift, but it holds my heart.
On Parents' Day we took a family photo together.
How could I ever repay all my parents' kindness?
Teachers' Day is May 15th.
grammar: 스승의날 (seuseung-ui nal) = Teachers' Day; 십오일 = the 15th (Sino).

english: On Teachers' Day we give our teacher a carnation.
It's a day to thank our teachers.
grammar: 감사드리다 (gamsadeurida) = to give thanks, humbly, to someone above you.

english: The classmates wrote a letter together.
Teacher, thank you for always teaching us.
We all sing 'Seuseung-ui Eunhye' together.
grammar: 은혜 (eunhye) = grace, kindness; the classic Teachers' Day song is named for it.

english: The teacher smiled brightly.
grammar: 웃으셨어요 (useusyeosseoyo) = smiled, with honorific -(으)시- for the teacher.

english: After graduating, we visit our teacher.
grammar: 찾아뵈다 (chajaboeda) = to visit an elder respectfully.

english: I'm truly grateful to have met a good teacher.
On Teachers' Day I think of my old homeroom teacher.
grammar: 생각나다 → 생각나요 (saenggangnayo) = comes to mind, I remember.

english: In Korea we eat seaweed soup on birthdays.
grammar: 미역국 (miyeokguk) = seaweed soup, eaten on birthdays and after childbirth.

english: Mother cooked seaweed soup for me.

target: 생일 아침에 미역국 한 그릇을 먹어요.
english: On my birthday morning I eat a bowl of seaweed soup.
Happy birthday, Minsu.
grammar: 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukhahaeyo) = happy birthday, in polite 해요체.

english: We put candles on the cake and light them.

target: 다 같이 생일 축하 노래를 불러요.
english: Everyone sings the birthday song together.
Blowing out the candles, I make a wish.
My friends prepared a surprise party.
I'm so happy to get the presents.
On birthdays my family cooks seaweed soup for me.
This year my birthday is on the weekend, which is nice.
Hwangap is the sixtieth birthday.
grammar: 환갑 (hwangap) = the big 60th-birthday celebration; 예순 살 = 60 years old.

english: We threw a big feast for Grandfather's 60th.
We invited all the relatives to the 70th-birthday feast.

target: 생일 케이크를 다 같이 나눠 먹었어요.
english: We shared the birthday cake all together.
My friend gave me a book as a birthday present.
Every birthday I call my parents.
grammar: -마다 (-mada) = every: 생일마다 = every birthday.

english: It feels sad not to eat seaweed soup on your birthday.
The candles on the cake are so pretty.
The birthday party was really fun.
grammar: 즐겁다 → 즐거웠어요 (jeulgeowosseoyo): a ㅂ-irregular past.

english: It's my younger sibling's birthday, so I bought a cake.
I got a lot of happy-birthday texts.
A birthday spent with family is the happiest.
The first doljanchi is a baby's first birthday.
grammar: 첫돌 (cheotdol) = a baby's first birthday, a big milestone in Korea.

english: For the first birthday we throw a big doljanchi.
grammar: 돌잔치 (doljanchi) = the first-birthday party held for the baby.

english: We invited the relatives to the doljanchi.
The baby wore a pretty hanbok.
At the doljanchi the baby does the doljabi.
grammar: 돌잡이 (doljabi) = the baby grabs an object to foretell its future.

english: At the doljabi the baby grabbed the pencil.
grammar: In 돌잡이 (doljabi) the grabbed object foretells the future: 연필 (yeonpil) = a scholar's path.

english: They say if the baby grabs the pencil, it'll study well.
Grabbing the thread is said to mean a long life.
grammar: 실 (sil) = thread; in the doljabi it stands for long life.

english: We arranged the food beautifully on the doljanchi table.

target: 아기가 첫돌을 맞아서 온 가족이 기뻐해요.
english: The whole family is glad the baby has reached its first birthday.
grammar: 3rd-person feelings take -어하다: 온 가족이 기뻐해요 (gippeohaeyo = the family is happy).

english: Grandmother gave the baby a gold ring.
grammar: A first-birthday custom: elders give the baby a 금반지 (geumbanji = gold ring).

english: We took lots of photos at the doljanchi.
I'm thankful the baby has grown up healthy.

target: 돌잡이 순간에 다 같이 박수를 쳤어요.
english: At the doljabi moment everyone clapped together.
My friends came to celebrate the first birthday.
Before Seollal we clean the house spotless.
We add dumplings to the tteokguk and eat it.
We prepared a fruit set as a Chuseok gift.
grammar: 명절 선물 (myeongjeol seonmul) = holiday gifts exchanged with family and coworkers.

english: I'm really happy today.
grammar: 기쁘다 → 기뻐요 (gippeoyo): drop the ㅡ, add -어요.

english: I'm so happy to hear I passed.
I'm a little sad my friend is leaving.
grammar: 슬프다 → 슬퍼요 (seulpeoyo): the ㅡ drops before -어요.

english: That movie made me very sad.
I'm suddenly getting angry.
grammar: 화가 나다 (hwaga nada) = to get angry; the anger 화 "comes up."

english: I got angry because my friend broke a promise.
I'm envious of my friend.
grammar: 부럽다 → 부러워요 (bureowoyo): a ㅂ-irregular feeling word.

english: I'm really envious of my friend who went traveling.
I get so nervous before a presentation.
grammar: 긴장되다 → 긴장돼요 (ginjangdwaeyo): 되다 becomes 돼요, not 되요.

english: I'm very nervous because of the interview.
I'm worried about the exam results.
grammar: 걱정되다 → 걱정돼요 (geokjeongdwaeyo) = it worries me.

english: I'm a little worried about tomorrow's weather.
I'm excited at the thought of going on a trip.
grammar: 기대되다 → 기대돼요 (gidaedwaeyo) = I look forward to it.

english: I bought concert tickets and I'm really excited.
grammar: 신나다 → 신나요 (sinnayo) = to be excited, thrilled.

english: I get scared when I'm alone at night.
grammar: 무섭다 → 무서워요 (museowoyo): a ㅂ-irregular.

english: High places really scare me.
Living alone, I sometimes feel lonely.
grammar: 외롭다 → 외로워요 (oerowoyo): another ㅂ-irregular feeling word.

english: I miss my parents back home.
grammar: 그립다 → 그리워요 (geuriwoyo) = to miss, to long for.

english: There's a lot of work, so I'm having a hard time lately.
It's a shame the weekend is so short.
grammar: 아쉽다 → 아쉬워요 (aswiwoyo) = to feel it's a pity.

english: I got a compliment, so I feel good.
I made a mistake, so I'm a little embarrassed.
grammar: 창피하다 → 창피해요 (changpihaeyo) = to feel embarrassed.

english: I fought with my friend, so I feel bad.
It's finally over, so I feel relieved.
Looking at the baby's photos, I feel at peace.
grammar: 편안하다 → 편안해요 (pyeonanhaeyo) = to feel comfortable, at ease.

english: I have nothing to do this weekend, so I'm bored.
grammar: 심심하다 → 심심해요 (simsimhaeyo) = to be bored.

english: We're not communicating, and it's frustrating.
grammar: 답답하다 → 답답해요 (dapdaphaeyo) = to feel stifled or frustrated.

english: I'm with good people, so I'm happy.
A loud noise came out of nowhere and startled me.
grammar: 놀라다 → 놀랐어요 (nollasseoyo) = was startled, surprised.

english: I read my friend's letter and was moved.
grammar: 감동하다 → 감동했어요 (gamdonghaesseoyo) = to be touched, moved.

target: 일이 잘 안 풀려서 짜증이 나요.
english: Things aren't working out, so I'm getting annoyed.
grammar: 짜증이 나다 (jjajeungi nada) = to get irritated, annoyed.

english: I was disappointed by someone I trusted.
It was moving enough to bring tears.
I'm truly happy that I passed.
When my child laughs, I'm happy too.
I finished the presentation well, so I feel proud.
Eating alone, I feel a bit lonely.
My friend is moving away, and I feel a pang of sadness.
grammar: 서운하다 → 서운해요 (seounhaeyo) = to feel hurt or sad about a parting.

english: I got a surprise gift, so I'm in a good mood.
I rested well for once, so I feel refreshed.
I think this movie is fun.
grammar: ~것 같아요 (geot gatayo) softens a claim into "I think / it seems."

english: It looks like it'll rain today.
grammar: 비가 올 것 같아요 (olgeot gatayo) = it looks like it'll rain.

target: 그 사람이 좋은 사람인 것 같아요.
english: I think that person is a good person.
grammar: N + 인 것 같아요 (in geot gatayo) = seems to be N: 사람인 것 같아요 = seems to be a person.

target: 이 문제가 조금 어려운 것 같아요.
english: I think this problem is a bit hard.
I think it's right, in my view.
grammar: 맞는 것 같아요 (manneun geot gatayo) = it seems correct.

target: 길이 막혀서 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
english: The roads are jammed, so I think I'll be a little late.
grammar: 늦을 것 같아요 (neujeul geot gatayo) = I'll probably be late.

target: 이 옷이 저한테 잘 어울리는 것 같아요.
english: I think this outfit suits me well.
I think I've caught a cold after all.
grammar: 걸린 것 같아요 (gollin geot gatayo) = seems I've caught it.

target: 그 식당이 문을 닫은 것 같아요.
english: I think that restaurant has closed.
I think I'm a bit tired today.
I think this one is better.
I think the pronunciation is a little off.

target: 이 색깔이 더 예쁜 것 같아요.
english: I think this color is prettier.
I think the meeting will end soon.

target: 그 소식은 사실이 아닌 것 같아요.
english: I don't think that news is true.
grammar: 아닌 것 같아요 (anin geot gatayo) = it seems not to be (so).

target: 이 음식이 좀 매운 것 같아요.
english: I think this food is a bit spicy.
I think the child is sleepy.
I think this bag is expensive.
I think those two are dating.
I think the weather will be clear tomorrow.
I think I made a bit of a mistake.

target: 이 노래를 어디선가 들은 것 같아요.
english: I feel like I've heard this song somewhere.
I think we'll run short on time.

target: 저 사람은 한국 사람인 것 같아요.
english: I think that person is Korean.
I think there'll be a lot of customers today.

target: 이 신발이 조금 작은 것 같아요.
english: I think these shoes are a little small.
I think that plan is okay.
I think the rain will stop soon.
I don't think anyone is here.
I think it's easier than I expected.
Yes, that's exactly right.
grammar: 맞아요 (majayo) = that's right, agreeing with what was said.

english: Right, I think so too.
Yes, that's a good idea.
grammar: 그래요 (geuraeyo) = that's so / okay, from 그렇다.

english: Oh, is that so? I didn't know.
Right, it really is.
grammar: 그렇죠 (geureojyo) = right? / isn't it, seeking agreement politely.

english: That's right, it's a bit cold today.
Yes, what you said is right.
I really think that's so.
Okay, let's do it that way.
Right, I'm of the same mind.
You're right, I hadn't realized.
Yes, doing it that way is right.
Okay, then I'll do it that way.
grammar: -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) marks a promise by the speaker: 할게요 = I'll do it.

english: Right, that's more convenient.
Of course, I'm in favor too.
Yes, it really was a lovely day.
Right, Korean is really fun.
I see; now I understand.
grammar: 그렇군요 (geureokunyo) = ah, I see, taking in new information.

english: Yes, everything you said is right.
Okay, let's meet again next time.
In my opinion, this one is better.
grammar: 제 생각에는 (je saenggage-neun) = in my opinion, softening what follows.

target: 제 생각에는 조금 비싼 것 같아요.
english: In my opinion it seems a bit pricey.
My opinion is a little different.
grammar: 의견 (uigyeon) = opinion; 제 의견은 = my opinion (topic).

english: I'm in favor of this plan.
I'm against that opinion.
grammar: 반대예요 (bandae-yeyo) = I'm opposed; the noun 반대 + 예요.

english: I agree on that point.
grammar: 동의하다 → 동의해요 (dong-uihaeyo) = to agree (formally).

english: Hmm, I'm not sure.
grammar: 글쎄요 (geulsseyo) = well… / hmm, hedging before an uncertain answer.

english: It's probably so.
grammar: 아마 (ama) = probably; it pairs with a guess like 그럴 거예요.

english: Of course, I'll gladly help.
grammar: 물론이에요 (mullon-ieyo) = of course, certainly.

english: Honestly, I'm not really into it.
grammar: 별로예요 (byeollo-yeyo) = not really, meh; a mild dislike.

english: In my opinion we need more time.
I don't think so.
grammar: -지 않다 (-ji anta) negates a verb: 생각하지 않아요 = I don't think (so).

english: In my opinion, both are fine.
Do you happen to have a different opinion?
grammar: 있으세요? (isseuseyo?) asks politely with honorific -(으)시- about the listener.

english: That's a good point, thank you.
In my opinion, right now is just right.
I relate to what you said, too.
grammar: 공감하다 → 공감해요 (gonggamhaeyo) = to relate, to empathize.

english: I'm fifty-fifty; it's hard to decide.

target: 제 생각에는 조금 이른 것 같아요.
english: In my opinion it seems a bit early.
May I give my honest opinion?
In my opinion this method is better.
I actually think the opposite.
Alright, I'll go with that opinion.
In my opinion there's no big problem.
Really? I had no idea at all.
grammar: 정말요? (jeongmaryo?) = really?, showing surprise politely.

english: In my opinion, let's wait a little longer.

target: 저는 이 색이 제일 마음에 들어요.
english: I like this color the best.
grammar: 마음에 들다 (maeume deulda) = to like, to be to one's taste.

target: 제 생각에는 그 말도 일리가 있어요.
english: In my opinion, that has a point too.
I'm not sure, but it's probably right.

target: 제 생각에는 다 함께 정하는 게 좋아요.
english: In my opinion it's best to decide all together.
That thought puts my mind at ease.
In my opinion this is enough as it is.
Either way is fine with me.
I'll share my thoughts honestly.

target: 결국 마음이 제일 중요한 것 같아요.
english: In the end, I think what's in the heart matters most.
The KTX is much faster than the bus.
grammar: 보다 attaches to the loser: A가 B보다 = A more than B — 버스보다 (beoseu-boda) = than the bus.

english: Planes are faster than trains.
Today is hotter than yesterday.
grammar: 더 is optional with 보다: 어제보다 (더) 더워요 (eoje-boda deo deowoyo) = hotter than yesterday.

english: The winter sea is quieter than the summer sea.
The cafe's coffee is stronger than the office coffee.
This bag is lighter than that one.
grammar: 가볍다 flips ㅂ to 우 before -어요: 가벼워요 (gabyeowoyo) = is light.

english: My older brother is two years older than me.
grammar: Ages compare with 살: 두 살 많아요 (du sal manayo) = is two years older.

english: My younger sibling sings better than I do.

target: 회사 근처 식당이 우리 동네 식당보다 비싸요.
english: Restaurants near the office are pricier than in my neighborhood.
Fruit is better for your health than snacks.
grammar: 건강에 좋아요 (geongang-e joayo) = good for your health — 에 marks what it's good for.

english: The subway is more comfortable than a taxi.
Our neighborhood is quieter than downtown.
The office is noisier than the cafe.
grammar: 시끄럽다 (noisy) is a ㅂ verb: ㅂ turns to 우 — 시끄러워요 (sikkeureowoyo).

english: The morning meeting is shorter than the afternoon one.
The office chairs are harder than the ones at home.
grammar: 딱딱해요 (ttakttakhaeyo) = hard, stiff — doubled syllables often mimic texture.

english: Spring weather is warmer than fall weather.
Seoul is much bigger than Busan.
grammar: 훨씬 (hwolssin) = by far: 훨씬 커요 = way bigger. Stronger than plain 더.

english: Korean class is more fun than I expected.
grammar: 생각보다 (saenggak-boda) = than I thought — a handy set phrase.

english: This cup is prettier than that cup.
A watermelon is heavier than an apple.
Our office is closer to the station.
The market is more crowded on weekends than on weekdays.
This hotel is cleaner than that hotel.
The bus takes longer than the subway.
Grandma's kimchi tastes better than store-bought.
My room is narrower than the living room.
grammar: 좁다 (jopda) = narrow, opposite of 넓다: 방이 좁아요 (bang-i jobayo) = the room is tight.

english: Friday evening is better than Monday morning.
I like winter more than summer.
grammar: Likes use 보다 too: 여름보다 겨울을 좋아해요 (yeoreum-boda) = prefer winter to summer.

english: I like bread more than rice.
Today's sky is clearer than yesterday's.
Today's meeting ran a little longer.
This room is brighter.
grammar: 밝다 (bakda) = bright: 방이 밝아요 (bang-i balgayo). Opposite: 어두워요 (dark).

english: Today is less cold than yesterday.
grammar: 덜 (deol) = less, the opposite of 더: 덜 추워요 = less cold.

english: The soup is less salty than yesterday.
This curry is less spicy than I expected.
Please speak a little more slowly.
grammar: -어 주세요 = do it for me: 말해 주세요 (malhae juseyo) = please say it.

english: Please turn the sound down a little.
I put more milk in my coffee.
grammar: 넣다 (neota) = put in: 우유를 넣어요 (uyu-reul neoeoyo) = add milk.

english: These days I work overtime less.
These days I drink more water.
I need a little more time.
I put in a little less sugar.
This place's tteokbokki is the best.
grammar: 제일 (jeil) + adjective = superlative: 제일 맛있어요 = the tastiest.

target: 우리 팀에서 지은 씨가 노래를 제일 잘해요.
english: Jieun sings the best on our team.
grammar: -에서 marks the group for superlatives: 우리 팀에서 (uri tim-eseo) = on our team.

target: 가족 중에서 아빠가 키가 제일 커요.
english: Dad is the tallest in the family.
grammar: 중에서 (jung-eseo) = among: 가족 중에서 = among the family.

target: 일 년 중에서 오월이 가장 좋아요.
english: May is my favorite month of the year.
grammar: 가장 (gajang) = 제일: 가장 좋아요 = like it most. 가장 sounds a touch more written.

english: Monday is the busiest day at work.

target: 우리 가족은 이 빵집을 제일 좋아해요.
english: Our family likes this bakery best.

target: 한국 음식 중에서 김치찌개를 제일 좋아해요.
english: Of Korean foods, I like kimchi stew best.
Jeju's sea is the most beautiful in Korea.
grammar: 아름답다 turns into 아름다워요 (areumdawoyo) — another ㅂ-to-우 adjective.

target: 겨울에는 이 온천이 제일 인기가 많아요.
english: In winter this hot spring is the most popular.
grammar: 인기가 많아요 (ingi-ga manayo) = is popular — literally 'has much popularity'.

target: 아침 지하철이 하루 중에서 가장 복잡해요.
english: The morning subway is the most crowded of the day.

target: 우리 팀에서 수진 씨가 제일 부지런해요.
english: Sujin is the most hardworking on our team.
Mom's voice is the warmest in the world.

target: 이 카페는 창가 자리가 제일 좋아요.
english: The window seats are the best at this cafe.
grammar: 창가 (changga) = by the window: 창가 자리 = window seat.

english: Strawberries are the sweetest fruit.
grammar: 달다 = sweet: 달아요 (darayo) — the ㄹ stays before -아요.

target: 우리 집에서 제 방이 제일 작아요.
english: My room is the smallest in our house.

target: 금요일 밤에는 이 거리가 가장 시끄러워요.
english: On Friday nights this street is the loudest.

target: 이 박물관이 우리 도시에서 제일 유명해요.
english: This museum is the most famous in our city.
Grandpa's stories are the most fun in the world.

target: 일주일 중에서 일요일 아침을 가장 좋아해요.
english: Sunday morning is my favorite time of the week.

target: 한 달 중에서 월급날이 제일 좋아요.
english: Payday is the best day of the month.
grammar: 월급날 (wolgeumnal — ㅂ before ㄴ sounds like ㅁ) = payday: 월급 (salary) + 날 (day).

english: My little sister sings like a pop star.
grammar: 처럼 (cheoreom) = like: 가수처럼 = like a singer. It glues right onto the noun.

english: The baby sleeps like an angel.
Today the sky is pretty as a picture.
Dad laughs like a kid.
That hotel is huge, like a palace.

target: 민수 씨는 모델처럼 옷을 잘 입어요.
english: Minsu dresses like a model.
The time flew by like a dream.
grammar: 빨리 (ppalli) = quickly, the adverb of 빠르다: 빨리 갔어요 = went by fast.

english: This towel is soft as a cloud.
grammar: 부드럽다 becomes 부드러워요 (budeureowoyo) = is soft — textures, voices, even people.

english: The meeting room is quiet as a library.
My older brother cooks like a chef.
Mom's sweater is really soft.
This bread is a little hard.
The new comforter is really light.
My laptop bag is too heavy.
This book is thick as a dictionary.
grammar: 두껍다 → 두꺼워요 (dukkeowoyo) = is thick; the opposite is 얇아요 (thin).

english: Summer pants are thin.
This alley is very narrow.
The new office has high ceilings.
grammar: 높다 (nopda) = high: 천장이 높아요 (cheonjang-i nopayo) = the ceiling is high.

english: In winter the sun sits low.
This lake is really deep.
The new towels are white.
Our uniforms are blue.
That roof is green.
This apple is a really pretty color.
It's too dark inside my bag.
grammar: 어둡다 → 어두워요 (eoduwoyo) = is dark: 방이 어두워요 = the room is dark.

english: The kitchen light is really bright.
This plate is plastic.
grammar: Materials just take the copula: 플라스틱이에요 (peullaseutik-ieyo) = it's plastic.

english: This desk is wood.
The meeting-room table is glass.
The new sofa is comfortable as a bed.
This blanket is really warm.
The plate is round like a full moon.
grammar: 둥글다 (dunggeulda) = round: 둥글어요 (dunggeureoyo). 보름달 = full moon.

english: This box is heavier than it looks.
The living-room window is really big.
These sneakers are light as a feather.
My phone screen is too dark.
The new office is really spacious.
The music in this cafe is quiet.
The market alleys are packed every weekend.
grammar: 마다 (mada) = every: 주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend.

english: Our neighborhood park is really clean.
grammar: 깨끗하다 (kkaekkeutada) = clean: 공원이 깨끗해요 = the park is clean.

english: This library is quiet in the afternoon.
The underground parking garage is dark.
The mountain air is really fresh.
The seawater is still cold.
The office is brighter in the afternoon.
In the countryside sky there are so many stars.
The road near the river is quiet.
My grandma's heart is wide as the sea.
grammar: 마음이 넓어요 (maeum-i neolbeoyo) = big-hearted — literally 'heart is wide'.

english: My uncle has broad shoulders.
Jieun has long hair.
grammar: Describe people with body word + adjective: 머리가 길어요 (meori-ga gireoyo) = has long hair.

english: Minsu is a generous host.
grammar: 손이 커요 (son-i keoyo), literally 'has big hands' = cooks and serves generously.

english: The baby's cheeks are soft as a peach.
Our team lead has a gentle voice.
grammar: Honor a 님-titled boss's trait with -(으)세요: 목소리가 부드러우세요 (budeureouseyo) = has a gentle voice.

english: My little brother has a sunny personality.
grammar: 성격이 밝아요 (seonggyeok-i balgayo) = has a bright, cheerful personality.

english: My friend has really big eyes.

target: 아빠는 키가 크고 엄마는 키가 작아요.
english: Dad is tall and Mom is short.
grammar: -고 (-go) links sentences: 크고 (keugo) = is tall and…

english: Grandpa is young at heart.
Sujin has a pretty smile.
The new house's living room is bright and spacious.
This neighborhood is quiet and safe at night.
The Jeju wind is really strong.
grammar: 세다 (seda) = strong: 바람이 세요 (baram-i seyo) = the wind is strong.

english: The winter mountains are beautiful as a painting.
Our company building is really tall.
Hello, I'd like to check in.
grammar: 체크인하다 = to check in — a Konglish verb: 체크인하고 싶어요 (chekeuinhago sipeoyo).

english: I booked under the name Kim Sujin.
grammar: (으)로 marks the means: 이름으로 (ireum-euro) = under the name.

english: I'm staying two nights, three days.
grammar: Nights and days count with Sino numbers: 2박 3일 (i-bak sam-il) = 2 nights, 3 days.

english: An ocean-view room, please.
grammar: 부탁해요 (butakaeyo) = please, I request it — softer than a command.

english: Is breakfast included?
grammar: 조식 (josik) = hotel breakfast — the check-in word, not everyday 아침.

english: What time does breakfast start?
I got two keys.
What's the wi-fi password here?
Where is the elevator?
I left my bags at the front desk.
grammar: 맡기다 (matgida) = leave in someone's care: 짐을 맡겨요 = check your bags.

english: Checkout is at eleven.
grammar: Clock hours use native numbers: 열한 시 (yeolhan si) = eleven o'clock.

english: I'd like to stay one more night.
grammar: 묵다 (mukda) = to stay the night: 하루 더 묵어요 = stay a day longer.

english: The pension is right in front of the sea.
grammar: 펜션 (pensyeon) = vacation guesthouse — a Korean family-trip staple.

english: You can see the sea from the room.
grammar: 보이다 = be visible: 바다가 보여요 (bada-ga boyeoyo) = the sea is in view.

english: The room is really clean.
The bed is really plush.
grammar: 푹신해요 (puksinhaeyo) = soft and cushy — the hotel-review word.

english: You can see the mountains from the window.
The kids went to the pool in the morning.
The front desk is on the first floor.
After checkout I waited in a cafe.
The hotel even has a hot spring.
I ordered dinner from room service.
The hotel breakfast was really good.

target: 일찍 도착했어요. 방이 아직 준비 중이에요.
english: I arrived early. The room is still being prepared.
grammar: N 중이에요 = in the middle of N: 준비 중이에요 (junbi jung-ieyo) = being prepared.

target: 경치가 좋아요. 그래서 이 펜션을 골랐어요.
english: The view is great. That's why I picked this pension.
grammar: 고르다 (choose) is 르-irregular: 골라요 (gollayo), past 골랐어요.

english: There's a problem with my reservation.
Please check the reservation again.
The date is wrong.
grammar: 틀리다 (teullida) = be wrong: 틀렸어요 = it's wrong.

target: 더블 룸을 예약했어요. 그런데 트윈 룸이에요.
english: I booked a double room, but it's a twin.
grammar: 그런데 (geureonde) = but, however — it starts the plot-twist sentence.

target: 방이 너무 추워요. 히터가 안 돼요.
english: The room is too cold. The heater doesn't work.
grammar: 안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) = it doesn't work — the complaint essential.

english: The wi-fi isn't working.
The shower water isn't hot.
The room next door is too loud.
Please change me to a different room.
I'd like to cancel my reservation.
Is there a cancellation fee?
grammar: 수수료 (susuryo) = fee, commission — the small-print word.

english: I'd like to check out a day early.
I need a receipt for my business trip.
Sorry, I misread the date.
grammar: 잘못 (jalmot) + verb = did it wrong: 잘못 봤어요 = looked at it wrong.

english: The staff were kind. They helped right away.
grammar: 금방 (geumbang) = right away, in no time.

english: Last month I traveled around Jeju Island.
I hiked up Hallasan. The view was the best.
grammar: 최고 (choego) = the best: 최고였어요 = it was the best.

english: I took a hundred photos at the beach.
grammar: 장 (jang) counts flat things: 사진 백 장 (sajin baek jang) = 100 photos.

english: The Jeju black pork was amazing.
grammar: 흑돼지 (heukdwaeji) = Jeju's famous black pig — an island specialty.

english: In the morning I watched the sunrise over the sea.
I walked the Olle Trail for three hours.
grammar: 올레길 (ollegil) = Jeju's network of seaside walking trails.

english: The wind was so strong my hat flew away.
grammar: -어서 = so, because: 세서 (seseo) = because it was strong.

english: I sent Grandma a box of tangerines.
grammar: 께 (kke) = honorific 'to': 할머니께 (halmeoni-kke) = to Grandma.

english: In Busan I tried raw fish for the first time.
grammar: -어 봤어요 = have tried: 먹어 봤어요 (meogeo bwasseoyo) = tried eating.

english: I swam in the sea at Haeundae.
The night view at Gwangalli was really beautiful.
grammar: 야경 (yagyeong) = night view — the word for city lights after dark.

english: I looked around at the fish in Jagalchi Market.
The Busan dialect is fun.
grammar: 사투리 (saturi) = regional dialect — Busan's is famously punchy.

english: I took a boat to an island.
The color of the sea was so pretty.
I ate a seed hotteok at the market.
grammar: 씨앗호떡 (ssiat-hotteok) = Busan's seed-stuffed hotteok — street-food royalty.

english: I took a slow walk to the lighthouse with my parents.
I made a new friend at the guesthouse.
On the last day of the trip I bought souvenirs.
Next time I'll come with my family.
I took the KTX from Seoul Station.
It takes about three hours to Busan.
grammar: 쯤 (jjeum) = about: 세 시간쯤 = around three hours.

english: I booked a window seat.
I bought my business-trip train ticket on the app.
The train left right on time.
grammar: 정각 (jeonggak) = exactly on the hour: 정각에 = right on time.

english: I ate a boxed lunch on the KTX.
The man in the next seat was friendly.
The tunnel was really long.
I kept watching the scenery out the window.
grammar: 풍경 (punggyeong) = scenery: 창밖 풍경 = the view outside the window.

english: The train stopped briefly in Daejeon.
grammar: 서다 (seoda) = to stop, stand: 섰어요 (seosseoyo) = it stopped.

english: I slept soundly on the train.
grammar: 푹 (puk) = deeply: 푹 잤어요 = slept like a log.

english: I was late and missed the train.
I switched to a ticket for the next train.
A round-trip ticket is more convenient than a one-way.
grammar: 왕복 (wangbok) = round trip; 편도 (pyeondo) = one way. 편도보다 = than one-way.

english: Train travel is more comfortable than bus travel.
My last vacation was so much fun.
grammar: 즐겁다 → 즐거워요 (jeulgeowoyo) = is enjoyable; past 즐거웠어요.

english: It rained on the first day of the trip.
The next day the weather was clear.
We got up early every morning.
We got lost once.
grammar: 한 번 (han beon) = one time; written as one word, 한번 = 'just try it'.

english: A kind lady showed us the way.
grammar: 길을 가르쳐 줘요 = show the way — 가르치다 isn't just for school.

english: I tried lots of local food.
grammar: 현지 (hyeonji) = local, on-site: 현지 음식 = local food.

english: I left my sunglasses at the hotel.
grammar: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = left it behind — put it down and came.

english: I took so many photos.
At night we looked around the market.
The kids loved the fireworks.
I got home and went straight to bed.
I made so many memories.
grammar: 추억 (chueok) = cherished memory: 추억이 생겨요 = memories come to be.

english: My legs hurt. Still, I was happy.
grammar: 그래도 (geuraedo) = even so, still — the comeback word.

english: This trip was shorter than the last one.
I practiced a lot of Korean during the trip.
After my business trip I traveled two more days.
grammar: 이틀 (iteul) = two days — a native word, like 하루 (one day).

english: I wrote about the trip on my blog.
You should definitely go to Busan.
grammar: -어 보세요 = give it a try: 가 보세요 (ga boseyo) = try going. 꼭 = definitely.

english: Try the Jeju tangerine juice.
You have to walk the Olle Trail.
Give this song a listen.
grammar: 들어 보세요 (deureo boseyo) = have a listen — 듣다's ㄷ turns into ㄹ.

english: Try sitting by the window.
Try on a hanbok.
grammar: 한복 (hanbok) = traditional Korean dress — rental shops cluster near the palaces.

english: You must try the market gimbap.
Go see the sea early in the morning.
Try riding the KTX once.

target: 이 여행 앱을 한번 써 보세요.
english: Give this travel app a try.
grammar: 써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try using it — 쓰다 covers both write and use.

english: Try learning a little dialect.
Try taking a photo here.
Try reading this travel book.
Ask the hotel staff.
grammar: 물어보다 = to ask: 물어보세요 (mureoboseyo) = go ahead and ask.

english: Check out the night market.
I packed my travel bag in advance.
grammar: 챙기다 (chaenggida) = pack, gather up: 짐을 챙겨요 = pack your things.

english: I pack my passport first.
grammar: 부터 (buteo) = starting with: 여권부터 = passport first.

english: I put my clothes in the suitcase.
grammar: 캐리어 (kaerieo) = rolling suitcase — Konglish, from 'carrier'.

english: I forgot my charger.
I put an umbrella in my bag too.
I packed a swimsuit and a hat.
grammar: 하고 (hago) = and, between nouns: 수영복하고 모자 = swimsuit and hat.

english: I made sure to pack cold medicine too.
The luggage was heavier than I expected.
I only took half my clothes.
grammar: 만 (man) = only: 반만 (ban-man) = only half.

english: I sent the trip photos to my family.

target: 이 사진 좀 보세요. 노을이 정말 예뻐요.
english: Look at this photo. The sunset glow is so pretty.
grammar: 노을 (noeul) = sunset glow — the pink-orange sky, not the sun itself.

english: I organized the photos on my computer.
I put the family photo on my desk.
I've already made plans for the next trip.
grammar: 계획을 세워요 (gyehoek-eul sewoyo) = make a plan — literally 'stand a plan up'.

english: This time I'm going to try Gyeongju.
grammar: -어 볼 거예요 = will give it a try: 가 볼 거예요 (ga bol geoyeyo) = will try going.

target: 여행 전에 한국어를 더 연습할 거예요.
english: I'll practice more Korean before the trip.
Traveling the world is my dream.
